Cognitive Psychology · Theme 6 · Complete reading summary

Judgment & decision making

Heuristics, biases, fallacies, expected utility, prospect theory and framing: every concept, study and example

Dear Sezen,

Theme 6 asks two questions that sound simple: how do we judge how likely something is, and how do we choose? The surprising answer from fifty years of research is that we rarely calculate. We use heuristics: quick rules of thumb that usually work, but that produce predictable errors (biases and fallacies). The second surprise is that the way a choice is described can flip our decision, even when the options are mathematically identical.

Your five readings fit together: Eysenck & Keane set up judgement (Bayes, base rates, representativeness, availability, natural frequencies); Matlin & Farmer deepen availability, illusory correlation and anchoring; Sternberg covers bounded rationality, satisficing, elimination by aspects and a catalogue of biases and fallacies; Matlin explains framing, overconfidence and hindsight; Robinson-Riegler contrasts expected utility with prospect theory and adds emotion.

This is your everyday work: hiring panels anchor on the first CV, ‘culture fit’ can hide representativeness and illusory correlations, defaults decide who joins a programme, and how you frame a transformation (‘what we gain’ vs ‘what we lose’) changes how people take risks.

How to read this platform. The Lessons panel has four tabs: 📖 Full lectures (43 screens, reading by reading, every concept and study), 🎯 Learning objectives (A–C judgement, D–E decision making, each answered), 🧩 Jigsaw topics (the ten one-minute expert topics) and 🧠 In-depth questions (all 16 tutorial questions with triage and a hidden model answer). On every screen look at the diagram first, read the bullets, say the hook out loud, then open the chips. Numbers marked illustrative or computed are labelled; all others come from your readings.

— Your professor

🍳 The big picture in one paragraph: Imagine your mind has two cooks. Cook 1 (Type 1 / System 1) is fast: he glances at the ingredients and says ‘looks like soup’. Cook 2 (Type 2 / System 2) is slow: he reads the recipe and weighs everything. Most of the time Cook 1 runs the kitchen, using shortcuts: does this look typical? (representativeness), how easily does an example come to mind? (availability), start from a number and adjust (anchoring). These shortcuts are usually good enough, but they ignore some information, so they fail in predictable ways. In decisions, Cook 1 also reacts to how the menu is written: ‘200 saved’ tastes different from ‘400 die’. Expected utility theory describes the ideal cook; prospect theory describes the real one.

📚 Key Terms: read these first

TermPlain-language definition
JudgmentEstimating how likely something is, using incomplete information.
Decision makingChoosing one option from several.
HeuristicA rule of thumb that ignores part of the information to decide quickly.
Bias / fallacyA systematic error that a heuristic (or motive) produces.
Base rateHow common something is in the population.
Normative vs descriptiveHow we *should* decide vs how we *actually* decide.
Bayesian inferenceUpdating prior beliefs (base rates) with evidence (likelihood ratio) to get posterior probabilities
Base-rate informationThe relative frequency of an event within a population
Representativeness heuristicJudging probability or category membership by similarity to what is typical
Availability heuristicJudging frequency by how easily examples come to mind
Anchoring and adjustmentStarting from an initial value and adjusting too little
Affect heuristicUsing one’s feelings (e.g. dread) to make quick judgements
Recognition heuristicIf you recognise one of two options, judge it to be larger or more frequent
Conjunction fallacyJudging A and B together as more likely than A alone
Illusory correlationBelieving two variables are related when they are not
Overconfidence / hindsight biasConfidence exceeds accuracy / ‘I knew it all along’ after the outcome
Gambler’s fallacy / hot handExpecting a random streak to reverse / to continue
Sunk-cost fallacyContinuing because of past, unrecoverable investment
Bounded rationality, satisficingRational within limits; choosing the first good-enough option (Simon)
Elimination by aspectsFiltering options on one attribute at a time (Tversky)
Expected utility theoryNormative model: choose the option with the highest utility × probability
InvariancePreferences should not depend on how options are presented
Prospect theoryDescriptive model: outcomes valued as gains/losses from a reference point; losses loom larger
Framing effectThe presentation or wording of options changes the choice

🧵 Synthesis

One thread runs through Theme 6: people replace hard questions with easy ones. Instead of ‘what is the probability?’ we ask ‘is it typical?’ (representativeness), ‘can I think of examples?’ (availability), ‘what number did I start from?’ (anchoring) or ‘how do I feel?’ (affect). Instead of ‘what is the best option?’ we ask ‘is this good enough?’ (satisficing) or ‘does it pass this one cut-off?’ (elimination by aspects). And instead of valuing final outcomes we ask ‘is this a gain or a loss from where I am?’ (prospect theory).

These substitutions are usually adaptive (Gigerenzer’s fast-and-frugal view), but they ignore information, so they fail predictably (Kahneman and Tversky’s biases): base rates, sample size and the conjunction rule disappear, memory distorts frequency, anchors stick, and the frame flips choices. Exam tip: for every bias, name the heuristic behind it, the information it ignores, a classic study with a number, and a fix (natural frequencies, the 2 × 2 table, reframing, considering alternatives).

Readings: Eysenck & Keane (pp. 622–631) · Matlin & Farmer (pp. 463–472) · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501) · Matlin (pp. 436–446) · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 481–489).

Lecture 1 of 43 · objectives J1 · D1

⚖️ Judgement and decision-making: the basics

Two overlapping skills, and why outcomes can mislead

❓ This lecture answers: What is the difference between judging how likely something is and deciding what to do, and why can a good decision still end badly?
↳ How it fits: This sets up the whole theme: first we look at how people guess chances (judgement), then at how they use those guesses to choose (decision-making).
  • Judgement = estimating the likelihood of events using incomplete information; what matters is accuracy.
  • Decision-making = selecting one option from several; complexity depends on the importance of the decision.
  • Judgement is usually an initial part of decision-making (judge each car’s costs, reliability, enjoyment, then choose).
  • Problem solving differs: there you generate your own solutions instead of choosing from given options.
  • Don’t judge a decision only by its outcome: a decision can be good given the information available, even if the result is bad.
🪝 Memory hook: Judge = ‘how likely?’ 🎲 · Decide = ‘which one?’ 🔀
★ KEY INSIGHT · Judgement estimates probabilities; decision-making chooses between options, often using those judgements.
Tap to open ▸
Judging is the weather forecast (‘70% chance of rain’). Deciding is whether you take the umbrella.
JudgementDecision-making
Core questionHow likely is X?Which option do I choose?
Informationincompleteoptions given; judgement needed if information is incomplete
Evaluated byaccuracyquality given the information (not only the outcome)
Examplechance of passing the next examwhich university or course to choose
▶ judgment vs decision making psychology▶ good decision bad outcome(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What is the key criterion for judgement?

Accuracy of the probability estimate.

Why is ‘the operation was a success, the patient died’ relevant?

A decision can be good given the information at the time even if the consequences are poor.

Part A · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 622–631)
Lecture 2 of 43 · objectives J2 · J3

🚕 Bayes’ theorem and the taxi-cab problem

How new evidence should change a belief

❓ This lecture answers: How should a perfectly logical thinker update a belief when new evidence arrives, as in the taxi-cab problem?
↳ How it fits: This gives the ‘statistician’ benchmark: Bayes’ rule says the base rate (how common something is) must always count, so we can measure how far real people stray from it.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SHOWS · base-rate neglectKahneman & Tversky (1972), taxi-cab problem: Do people combine how common Blue taxis are with what an 80%-accurate witness says?
  • New information changes how likely we think something is (90% sure someone lied → 60% after confirmation).
  • Bayesian inference: start with prior odds (beliefs before the data), multiply by the likelihood ratio (how probable the data are under each hypothesis).
  • Formula (odds form): p(HA|D)/p(HB|D) = [p(HA)/p(HB)] × [p(D|HA)/p(D|HB)].
  • Taxi-cab problem (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972): 15% Blue, 85% Green; witness says Blue and is right 80% of the time.
  • Answer: odds 12 : 17 → 41% Blue. Most people say 80%: they ignore the base rate.
🪝 Memory hook: Prior × evidence = posterior: the base rate always gets a vote 🗳️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A reliable witness is not enough when the event itself is rare: the base rate matters.
Tap to open ▸
Picture 100 cabs. Only 15 are blue. The witness will call 12 of them blue, but she will also wrongly call 17 green cabs blue. So of all ‘blue’ reports, only 12 out of 29 are really blue.
TermTaxi-cab value
Prior probability HA (Blue)0.15
Prior probability HB (Green)0.85
p(D|HA): says Blue when Blue0.80
p(D|HB): says Blue when Green0.20
Posterior odds0.12 : 0.17 = 12 : 17
Probability Blue12 / 29 ≈ 41%

🧪 Demo: Bayes calculator (natural frequencies)

Move the sliders. Watch how a rare event makes even a good test or witness unreliable.

Defaults = the taxi-cab problem (15% Blue, witness right 80%).

▶ Bayes theorem taxi cab problem▶ Bayes theorem explained simply(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What two ingredients does Bayes’ theorem combine?

Prior odds (base rates) and the likelihood ratio of the data under each hypothesis.

Why do most people answer 80%?

They use only the witness’s accuracy and ignore the 15% base rate.

Part A · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 622–631)
Lecture 3 of 43 · objectives J3 · J5

👷 Neglecting base rates

Taxi cabs and Jack the engineer

❓ This lecture answers: Do people actually use how common something is when they judge a case, or does a vivid description take over?
↳ How it fits: Here the theme’s question gets its first test: in the taxi-cab and Jack problems people mostly ignore the base rate, so they are not calculating like Bayes.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SHOWS · representativeness beats base ratesKahneman & Tversky (1973), lawyer-engineer problem: Does changing how many engineers are in the group change people's guess about Jack's job?
  • Base-rate information = the relative frequency of an event within a population.
  • Bayes says we must use it, but people often ignore or de-emphasise it.
  • Taxi-cab: most people answer 80%, using only the witness’s accuracy.
  • Lawyer–engineer problem: Jack’s description was drawn from 100 (70 engineers/30 lawyers, or the reverse).
  • People judged P(engineer) = .90 in both conditions: the 70 : 30 split was ignored.
🪝 Memory hook: Base rate = how many fish are in the pond 🐟; the description is just the one you caught.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A vivid description easily overrides how common something actually is.
Tap to open ▸
If 70 of 100 people in a room are lawyers, a random person is probably a lawyer, even if he likes puzzles. People forget the room and look only at the person.
📄 Kahneman & Tversky (1973): lawyer–engineer problem
ElementDetail
QuestionDo people use base rates when judging category membership?
MethodParticipants read Jack’s description, drawn at random from 100 descriptions; half were told 70 engineers / 30 lawyers, half 30 engineers / 70 lawyers.
FindingsMean judged probability that Jack was an engineer was .90 in both groups.
ConclusionBase rates were ignored; judgement was driven by how representative Jack was.
Why it mattersClassic demonstration of base-rate neglect.
▶ base rate fallacy explained▶ lawyer engineer problem Kahneman(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Define base-rate information.

The relative frequency of an event within a given population.

What would Bayes predict in the lawyer–engineer problem?

A higher probability of ‘engineer’ when 70 of the 100 are engineers than when only 30 are.

Lecture 4 of 43 · objectives J4 · J5

👩 Representativeness and the conjunction fallacy

Linda the bank teller

❓ This lecture answers: Why do people judge ‘feminist bank teller’ more likely than ‘bank teller’ for Linda, when that is logically impossible?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L3: the shortcut behind base-rate neglect is representativeness (judging by how typical something looks), and here it breaks a basic rule of probability.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SHOWS · conjunction fallacyTversky & Kahneman (1983), Linda: Will people judge two things together as more likely than one of them alone?
  • SUPPORTS · conjunction fallacy is not misunderstandingSides et al. (2002): Does the Linda error disappear when the wording is made completely unambiguous?
  • AGAINST · standard probability-based explanationTentori et al. (2013): Do people pick the added detail that is most probable, or the one the description supports?
  • SHOWS · intelligence does not protectStanovich (2011): Are students with high SAT scores less likely to make the conjunction fallacy?
  • Representativeness heuristic: deciding something belongs to a category because it looks typical of it (Jack seems a typical engineer).
  • Conjunction fallacy: believing A and B together is more likely than A alone (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983).
  • Linda: most people say ‘feminist bank teller’ is likelier than ‘bank teller’, yet all feminist bank tellers are bank tellers.
  • Not just a misunderstanding: the fallacy remains when the wording is made unambiguous (Sides et al., 2002).
  • Tentori et al. (2013): the fallacy happens because the added information is strongly supported by the description, not because it is probable (black-shoes test).
🪝 Memory hook: A ⊂ B: the smaller circle can never win.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Adding details makes a story more convincing and less probable.
Tap to open ▸
‘Bank teller’ includes every bank teller, feminist or not. Adding ‘feminist’ can only shrink the group, but it makes the story fit Linda better, so it feels more likely.
Explanation of the fallacyPrediction for ‘bank teller who owns black shoes’Result
Standard (high probability of the added information)rated likelier than ‘feminist bank teller’ (black shoes are very common)not supported
Hypothesis support (Tentori et al., 2013)rated less likely: the description doesn’t support ‘black shoes’supported
Other examples (Matlin & Farmer)Why it’s a fallacy
‘murders in Detroit’ judged higher than ‘murders in Michigan’Detroit is inside Michigan
‘spilling hot coffee’ seems likelier than ‘spilling coffee’hot coffee is a subset of coffee
Students with high SAT scores show the fallacy MORE (Stanovich, 2011)intelligence doesn’t protect you
▶ Linda problem conjunction fallacy▶ representativeness heuristic(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why is ‘feminist bank teller’ less probable than ‘bank teller’?

It is a conjunction: a subset of all bank tellers, so it can never be more probable.

What did Tentori et al. (2013) show?

The fallacy arises because the added hypothesis is strongly supported by the description, not because it is highly probable.

Part A · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 622–631)
Lecture 5 of 43 · objectives J3 · J5

🩺 Heuristics in medical experts

McKinley, double conjunctions and diagnostic biases

❓ This lecture answers: Do experts such as doctors also fall for the ‘looks typical’ shortcut, and what diagnostic mistakes does it cause?
↳ How it fits: This shows the shortcuts are not just a student lab effect: even trained medical experts judge by resemblance and make costly errors.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SHOWS · representativeness in expertsDr Croskerry and the forest ranger (Groopman, 2007): Can a fit, healthy look lead an experienced doctor to miss a heart problem?
  • SUPPORTS · hypothesis-support account; experts not immuneCrupi et al. (2018): Do medical experts judge two disorders together as likelier than each one alone?
  • SHOWS · biases in medical diagnosisSaposnik et al. (2016); Croskerry (2018): How often are biases like anchoring and overconfidence linked to errors in medical decisions?
  • Experts also use representativeness wrongly: Dr Croskerry dismissed a fit forest ranger’s chest pain; he had a heart attack shortly after (Groopman, 2007).
  • Croskerry: ‘my thinking was overly influenced by how healthy this man looked’.
  • Double conjunction fallacy: judging A + B more probable than A and than B separately. 49% of medical experts did so (Crupi et al., 2018).
  • Fits Tentori’s hypothesis explanation: the evidence strongly supported both disorders together.
  • Common medical biases: anchoring, omission bias, overconfidence; linked to inaccuracies in 36–77% of cases.
🪝 Memory hook: Looks healthy ≠ is healthy: experts judge by resemblance too.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Expertise doesn’t protect against heuristic errors.
Tap to open ▸
Even a good doctor thought ‘he looks way too healthy for a heart problem’. That’s the representativeness heuristic, and it nearly cost a life.
BiasDefinitionMedical example
Representativenessjudging by similarity to a typical case‘healthy-looking’ patient’s chest pain dismissed
Double conjunction fallacyA + B judged more probable than A and than B alonealcoholism and thalassemia (49% of experts)
Anchoringrelying too much on the first symptom identifiedsticking to the first diagnosis
Omission biaspreferring inaction over actionnot treating
Overconfidenceexcessive confidence in one’s judgementno second look
▶ cognitive bias in medicine diagnosis▶ double conjunction fallacy(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What is the difference between the conjunction and the double conjunction fallacy?

Double: A + B is judged more probable than A AND more probable than B separately; the single version compares with one of them.

Why did McKinley’s case show representativeness?

He looked like a typical healthy, low-risk person, so the doctor ignored the possibility of heart disease.

Part A · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 622–631)
Lecture 6 of 43 · objectives J2 · J3

🧠 Heeding base rates

Causal stories and motivation bring base rates back

❓ This lecture answers: When do people take base rates seriously after all: what do causal stories and personal motivation change?
↳ How it fits: This softens L3: base-rate neglect is not fixed, it shrinks when people understand why false results happen or have a reason to doubt the evidence.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • MIXED · partial use of base ratesBialek (2017): Do people use the base rate when it is very extreme, such as 997 out of 1,000?
  • AGAINST · base-rate neglect as fixed flawKrynski & Tenenbaum (2007): Do people use base rates once the problem explains why a false alarm can happen?
  • SHOWS · motivation and myside biasDitto et al. (1998): Do people use a test's error rate more when the test gives them bad news?
  • People make some use of base rates: P(engineer) .84 when 997/1,000 were engineers vs .53 when 3/1,000 (Bialek, 2017); some even use irrelevant base rates.
  • Krynski & Tenenbaum (2007): we have causal knowledge that lab problems fail to provide.
  • Mammogram (2% cancer; 6% false positives): base rate neglected, but a benign-cyst wording (a cause for false positives) made people use it.
  • Faded-paint taxi version: base-rate neglect 43% → 8%; correct answers 8% → 46%.
  • Motivation: people use base rates when the result is bad news for them (Ditto et al., 1998); cf. myside bias.
🪝 Memory hook: Give people the ‘why’ (a cause) and the base rate suddenly matters.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Base-rate neglect shrinks when people understand the causal structure or are motivated to doubt.
Tap to open ▸
If you are told some healthy women have a cyst that looks like cancer, you naturally think ‘so a positive might just be the cyst’, and you use the numbers properly.
📄 Krynski & Tenenbaum (2007)
ElementDetail
QuestionDo people use base rates when the causal structure is clear?
MethodMammogram problem with a standard false-positive wording vs a benign-cyst wording; taxi problem with a ‘faded paint’ explanation of witness errors.
FindingsBenign-cyst version: base rates used far more. Faded paint: base-rate neglect 43% → 8%; correct 8% → 46%.
ConclusionBase-rate neglect partly reflects missing causal knowledge in lab problems.
Why it mattersLab tasks may exaggerate our irrationality.
StudyFinding
Bialek (2017).84 vs .53 for 997 vs 3 engineers out of 1,000
Ditto et al. (1998)bad news → people use the 1-in-10 error base rate to dismiss the test; good news → test seen as accurate
▶ base rate neglect causal reasoning▶ myside bias(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What did the faded-paint version change?

It explained why the witness might err, so far fewer people neglected the base rate (8% vs 43%).

What is myside bias?

Favouring information consistent with one’s prior beliefs over information that contradicts them.

Lecture 7 of 43 · objectives J2 · J4

💭 Availability and the affect heuristic

Ease of recall, dread and familiarity

❓ This lecture answers: How do ease of recall and feelings of dread shape our sense of how common or risky something is?
↳ How it fits: This adds a second shortcut, availability: instead of counting, we let what comes to mind easily, or what scares us, stand in for real frequency.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · availabilityLichtenstein et al. (1978): Do people judge widely reported causes of death as more common than quieter ones?
  • SUPPORTS · availability and the affect heuristicPachur et al. (2012): What best predicts people's guesses about causes of death: own experience, dread or media?
  • SUPPORTS · affect heuristicScherer et al. (2018): Does reading about a product's harms change how people feel about it and judge its benefits?
  • SHOWS · familiarity makes statements feel trueFazio et al. (2015): Does seeing a false statement before make it feel truer, even when people know better?
  • SHOWS · System 2 can override availabilityOppenheimer (2004); Oppenheimer & Monin (2009): Do people always pick the name that comes to mind most easily as the more common one?
  • Availability heuristic: estimate frequency by how easily instances are retrieved from long-term memory.
  • Publicised causes of death (murder) judged likelier than less publicised ones (suicide), even when the opposite is true (Lichtenstein et al., 1978).
  • Pachur et al. (2012): availability from direct experience best predicted judged risks; the affect heuristic (dread) also predicted them; media-based availability was the weakest.
  • Familiar statements feel truer even when you know better (Fazio et al., 2015).
  • Availability can be overridden by deliberate thought, but under cognitive load people fall back on it (80%; Oppenheimer & Monin, 2009).
🪝 Memory hook: Easy to recall → feels common. Scary → feels common.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Ease of recall and feelings of dread stand in for real frequencies.
Tap to open ▸
Ask people what kills more people and they name what they can picture or what scares them. That isn’t always what is actually most common.
HeuristicRuleEvidence
Availability (direct experience)judge by examples you have experiencedbest predictor of judged causes of death
Availability (total experience)own experience + mediaweakest predictor
Affect heuristicthe more dread, the more frequentalso predicted judgements; harm info lowers judged benefit (Scherer et al., 2018)
▶ availability heuristic examples▶ affect heuristic(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Which predictor of judged causes of death did best in Pachur et al. (2012)?

Availability based on recall of direct experiences.

How did Oppenheimer show that availability can be overridden?

People didn’t pick famous names as more common, but did so 80% of the time under cognitive load.

Lecture 8 of 43 · objectives J3 · J5

🏥 Availability in medicine and debiasing

Recent cases spring to mind, and how doctors can resist

❓ This lecture answers: How do recent cases push doctors into wrong diagnoses, and what can they do to resist the availability shortcut?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L7: availability errors happen in real clinics too, but structured reflection and listing alternatives show the shortcuts can be corrected.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SHOWS · availability in diagnosisDr Alter's aspirin case (Groopman, 2007): Can a run of recent pneumonia cases lead a doctor to misdiagnose a different illness?
  • SUPPORTS · availability in diagnosisMamede et al. (2010b): Do doctors repeat a recent diagnosis when a new case looks similar to earlier ones?
  • SUPPORTS · debiasing by guided reflectionLambe et al. (2016): Which kind of intervention best reduces doctors' diagnostic errors?
  • Dr Alter saw dozens of viral-pneumonia cases in three weeks, then misdiagnosed a woman with aspirin toxicity as pneumonia (Groopman, 2007).
  • Recent cases made pneumonia spring to mind, despite missing signs (no white streaks, no rhonchi).
  • Mamede et al. (2010b): doctors facing a case similar to recent ones wrongly gave the earlier diagnosis.
  • Best intervention: guided reflection (Lambe et al., 2016); also considering alternative diagnoses.
  • Heuristic against heuristics: ROWS = rule out the worst-case scenario (Croskerry, 2018).
🪝 Memory hook: Last week’s cases write this week’s diagnosis, unless you stop and list alternatives.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Structured reflection and forced alternatives reduce availability errors.
Tap to open ▸
If you have just treated twenty flu patients, the twenty-first cough also looks like flu. Good doctors force themselves to ask: what else could this be?
InterventionHow it works
Guided reflection (most effective)use guided, structured, reflective processes before deciding
Considering alternativesalways generate a short list of other diagnoses
ROWSfirst rule out the worst-case scenario
▶ diagnostic error availability bias▶ debiasing strategies medicine(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why did Dr Alter misdiagnose aspirin toxicity?

Many recent pneumonia cases made that diagnosis highly available.

What was the most effective debiasing intervention in Lambe et al. (2016)?

Guided reflection.

Part A · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 622–631)
Lecture 9 of 43 · objectives J1 · J4

🔎 Anchoring and evaluating the heuristics approach

What Kahneman & Tversky gave us, and what’s missing

❓ This lecture answers: What is anchoring, and what are the strengths and weaknesses of Kahneman and Tversky’s heuristics approach as a whole?
↳ How it fits: This steps back to judge the shortcut story itself: it found many errors but explains them vaguely, and some errors come from biased information rather than a faulty mind.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · anchoring-and-adjustmentFiedler & von Sydow (2015), roulette wheel: Does a random roulette-wheel number change estimates of African countries in the UN?
  • AGAINST · errors come from faulty processingHertwig et al. (2005): Why do people judge skin cancer as more common than mouth and throat cancer?
  • AGAINST · emotion-free heuristics accountLench & Darbor (2014): Does being in a sad mood change how risky people think formaldehyde is?
  • AGAINST · lab biases reflect everyday judgementMcDowell & Jacobs (2017): Are judgement biases as large in natural conditions as in artificial lab problems?
  • Anchoring-and-adjustment: make an initial estimate (anchor), adjust it, but too little (roulette wheel → UN countries).
  • Kahneman & Tversky founded judgement research; their ideas spread to decision-making, reasoning, economics and philosophy.
  • Limitations: heuristics are vaguely defined (‘theory surrogates’) and theory has progressed little.
  • Errors may come from a biased sample of information (media coverage of skin cancer), not from biased processing.
  • Emotion and motivation were long ignored; lab tasks may be artificial.
🪝 Memory hook: Five ways to criticise heuristics: Vague, Unprogressed, Sample, Emotion, Artificial (VUSEA).
★ KEY INSIGHT · Not every wrong judgement comes from a faulty mind; sometimes the information we receive is biased.
Tap to open ▸
Kahneman and Tversky’s labels are great for spotting errors but don’t really explain how the mind computes. And sometimes the mind is fine: it’s the information we are fed that is skewed.
LimitationExample
Heuristics vaguely defined‘representativeness’ places no testable constraints on the process
Limited theoretical progressanchoring may reflect priming rather than insufficient adjustment
Biased environment, not biased processingskin cancer judged commoner than mouth/throat cancer because of media coverage (Hertwig et al., 2005)
Emotion and motivation neglectedformaldehyde judged riskier in a sad mood (Lench & Darbor, 2014)
Artificial lab tasksbiases may be smaller in naturalistic conditions (McDowell & Jacobs, 2017)

Why are heuristics called ‘theory surrogates’?

One-word labels don’t specify the cognitive process or make testable predictions.

Give an example where an error comes from the environment, not the mind.

Overestimating skin-cancer deaths because of heavy media coverage.

Part A · Eysenck & Keane (pp. 622–631)
Lecture 10 of 43 · objectives J2

🔢 The natural frequency hypothesis

Counts beat percentages

❓ This lecture answers: Does presenting the same problem as counts (‘12 out of 29’) instead of percentages help people reason like Bayes?
↳ How it fits: This suggests people are better ‘statisticians’ than L3 implied: with natural frequencies, the format our minds evolved for, far more people get the answer right.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · natural-frequency hypothesisGigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995): Do more people solve a mammogram-type problem when it is given as counts, not percentages?
  • SUPPORTS · natural-frequency hypothesisMcDowell & Jacobs (2017), meta-analysis: Across many studies, do natural frequencies reliably beat probabilities for Bayesian reasoning?
  • SUPPORTS · natural frequencies help expertsHoffrage et al. (2015): Do advanced medical students also reason better with counts than with probabilities?
  • In daily life we rarely get summary statistics; we meet cases one by one: natural sampling.
  • Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995): evolution makes frequencies easy, fractions and percentages hard.
  • Mammogram-type problem: 16% correct with probabilities vs 46% with natural frequencies.
  • Meta-analysis (McDowell & Jacobs, 2017): clear advantage for frequencies; visual aids help both formats.
  • Even experts benefit: medical students 45% vs 7% (Hoffrage et al., 2015). Problems: samples are biased; word problems bypass natural sampling.
🪝 Memory hook: Say ‘12 out of 29’, not ‘0.41’.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The same Bayesian problem becomes much easier when presented as natural frequencies.

‘1% of women have cancer’ is hard to use. ‘10 out of 1,000 women have cancer; 8 of them test positive, and so do 95 healthy women’ is easy: 8 out of 103.

What is natural sampling?

Encountering instances of a population one after another, as in everyday life.

Name one problem for the natural frequency hypothesis.

Part B · Matlin & Farmer (pp. 463–472)
Lecture 11 of 43 · objectives J2 · J4

🧺 The availability heuristic (Matlin & Farmer)

Usually accurate, until recency and familiarity contaminate it

❓ This lecture answers: What exactly is the availability heuristic, and when does judging by ‘easy to think of’ give a good answer?
↳ How it fits: This shows availability is usually a sensible shortcut, because memory often mirrors reality; it only goes wrong when something else makes examples memorable.
  • Availability: estimate frequency or probability by how easily you can think of examples.
  • Generally helpful: you recall many Illinois students and one from Idaho, so ‘more from Illinois’ is a good guess.
  • Accurate as long as availability correlates with true frequency, and it usually does.
  • Errors arise when factors unrelated to frequency boost memory: recency and familiarity (Figure 12.2).
  • Rule of thumb: similarity judgement → representativeness; recalling examples → availability.
🪝 Memory hook: Availability is a memory search: whatever is easy to find feels frequent 🔍.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Availability works when memory mirrors reality and fails when something else makes examples memorable.
Tap to open ▸
If you ask yourself ‘are there more dogs or ferrets in my street?’, you count the ones you can remember. That works, unless you met a ferret yesterday and it’s all you can think about.
RepresentativenessAvailability
You are givena specific example (THTHHT, Linda)a general category (students from Illinois)
You judgeis the example similar to the category?can I easily recall examples?
Typical errorconjunction fallacy, base-rate and sample-size neglectrecency and familiarity distortions, illusory correlation

🧩 Comprehension check

When is the availability heuristic accurate?

When ease of recall is correlated with true, objective frequency.

How can you tell representativeness from availability in a question?

Similarity judgement → representativeness; recalling examples → availability.

Part B · Matlin & Farmer (pp. 463–472)
Lecture 12 of 43 · objectives J3

📰 Recency and familiarity

Why the news shapes our estimates

❓ This lecture answers: How do recent events and media coverage make some things feel more common than they really are?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L11: recency and familiarity are the two forces that make examples easy to recall without making them more frequent, which is where availability fails.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · recency distorts availabilityMacLeod & Campbell (1992): Does recalling pleasant or unpleasant past events change how likely similar future events seem?
  • SUPPORTS · familiarity distorts availabilityBrown & Siegler (1992): Does news coverage of a country change how big people think its population is?
  • SUPPORTS · familiarity distorts availabilityBrown, Cui & Gordon (2002): Do media distort population estimates in Canada, the US and China as well?
  • Recency: recent items are more available, so judged more likely (estimates of scandal-related crimes after the 2011 university scandal).
  • MacLeod & Campbell (1992): recalling pleasant past events made pleasant future events seem likelier; unpleasant → unpleasant.
  • Familiarity: media coverage distorts population estimates (Brown & Siegler, 1992): El Salvador ≈ Indonesia, although Indonesia was ≈35 × larger.
  • Media also shape perceived support for views (thousands of protesters vs a few dozen counter-protesters).
  • Counter it by switching from Type 1 to Type 2 processing: check the statistics.
🪝 Memory hook: Recent & familiar = loud in memory, not common in reality 📢.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Recency and familiarity make examples easy to recall without making them more frequent.
Tap to open ▸
After a week of plane-crash news, flying feels dangerous. Nothing changed about planes; only your memory got louder.

How can recency bias the availability heuristic?

Recent examples are easier to recall, so we judge them more frequent than they are.

How could therapists use MacLeod & Campbell’s finding?

Have depressed clients recall pleasant past events to make a hopeful future seem likelier.

🏙️ The recognition heuristic

When ignorance helps you choose

❓ This lecture answers: How can recognising only one of two options, such as Milan but not Modena, actually lead to a correct judgement?
↳ How it fits: This shows a shortcut that works well: when recognition goes along with size or importance, a little ignorance plus recognition gives accurate guesses.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · recognition heuristicGoldstein & Gigerenzer (2002), Milan vs Modena: When people know only one of two cities, do they pick it as bigger, and are they right?
  • SUPPORTS · recognition heuristicVolz et al. (2006): How accurate are judgements based on recognising one option but not the other?
  • A special case of the availability heuristic that typically leads to accurate decisions.
  • Rule: compare two categories; if you recognise one but not the other, the recognised one has the higher frequency.
  • Milan vs Modena: US students know Milan, not Modena → ‘Milan is bigger’ → correct.
  • It works because recognition is usually correlated with size or importance.
  • Example of a heuristic that is fast, frugal and good: part of the ‘current status’ debate (Gigerenzer).
🪝 Memory hook: Heard of it? Then it’s probably the bigger one.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Partial ignorance plus recognition can produce accurate judgements.
Tap to open ▸
If you only know one of two cities, it is probably the bigger one: big cities are talked about more. Not knowing the other actually helps you.

State the recognition heuristic.

If you recognise one of two categories but not the other, judge the recognised one to be more frequent.

Why is it usually accurate?

Recognition tends to be correlated with real size or frequency.

Part B · Matlin & Farmer (pp. 463–472)
Lecture 14 of 43 · objectives J5

🔲 Illusory correlation

Seeing relationships that aren’t there

❓ This lecture answers: Why do people see links between two things, such as a group and a behaviour, when the evidence shows none?
↳ How it fits: This shows how the availability shortcut feeds a bias: we notice one memorable cell of the evidence and ignore the rest, which helps keep stereotypes alive.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SHOWS · illusory correlationChapman & Chapman (1969): Do students see a link between inkblot answers and group membership that is not in the data?
  • SUPPORTS · distinctiveness drives illusory correlationRisen et al. (2007): Are combinations of a rare group and a rare behaviour especially memorable?
  • SHOWS · illusory correlationChapman & Chapman (1967-1975), Draw-a-Person: Do clinicians see signs like large eyes in drawings as linked to paranoia when no link exists?
  • Illusory correlation: believing two variables are statistically related when the evidence shows no relationship (or a much weaker one).
  • Many stereotypes rest on illusory correlations; the social-cognition view traces them to normal cognitive processes, especially availability.
  • To judge a relationship you need all four cells of a 2 × 2 matrix; people focus on one cell (6 of 60 vs 8 of 80: both 10%).
  • Rare + rare combinations are especially memorable (Risen et al., 2007); prejudice adds confirmation-seeking.
  • Chapman & Chapman (1969): students formed an illusory correlation between inkblot responses and group membership. Media and politicians often quote one cell (fraudulent welfare claims).
🪝 Memory hook: One cell is a story; four cells are evidence 🔲🔲🔲🔲.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A correlation can only be judged from all four cells of the table.
Tap to open ▸
‘I keep seeing people from group X with problem Y!’ But how many from group X don’t have it, and how many from other groups do? Without those numbers there is no correlation, just memorable cases.
Group XGroup Y

6/60 and 8/80 are both 10%.

What mistake creates most illusory correlations?

Attending to only one cell of the 2 × 2 matrix instead of all four.

Part B · Matlin & Farmer (pp. 463–472)
Lecture 15 of 43 · objectives J4 · J5

⚓ The anchoring and adjustment heuristic

Start somewhere, adjust too little

❓ This lecture answers: Why does the first number we see, even a random one, pull our estimate towards it?
↳ How it fits: This adds the ‘first number’ shortcut: we start from an anchor and adjust too little, which bends judgements even for experienced judges.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · anchoring-and-adjustmentTversky & Kahneman (1982), multiplication: Does starting with 8×7×6 rather than 1×2×3 change a five-second estimate of the product?
  • SUPPORTS · anchoring in expertsEnglich & Mussweiler (2001): Does a novice prosecutor's sentence demand change the sentence experienced judges give?
  • SUPPORTS · anchor precision affects adjustmentJaniszewski & Uy (2008): Do people adjust more from a round price like $3,000 than from a precise one like $2,991?
  • SUPPORTS · anchoring in real marketsBeggs & Graddy (2009): Do earlier sale prices pull later art auction prices towards them?
  • SUPPORTS · anchoring in real marketsCampbell & Sharpe (2009): Are experts' economic forecasts pulled towards last month's figures?
  • Start with a first approximation (anchor), then adjust using other information; the adjustment is too small (Tversky & Kahneman, 1982).
  • 8×7×…×1 → median 2,250; 1×2×…×8 → 512; true answer 40,320 (both anchored on single digits).
  • Works even with arbitrary or absurd anchors (living to 140), and in experts.
  • Experienced judges: a novice ‘prosecutor’ demanding 12 months → 28 months; 34 months → 36 (Englich & Mussweiler, 2001).
  • Likely mechanism: the anchor restricts memory search to nearby values. Related top-down tendencies: belief bias, confirmation bias, illusory correlation.
🪝 Memory hook: The first number drops an anchor ⚓; your estimate stays on a short rope.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Any number you see first, even a random one, pulls your estimate towards it.
Tap to open ▸
Ask for a quick estimate of 8×7×6×5×4×3×2×1 and people start from big numbers; start from 1×2×3… and they start small. Both stop far too early, because they never move far from where they started.

Why were both multiplication estimates too low?

People anchored on the first single digits and adjusted too little.

What is the likely mechanism of anchoring?

The anchor restricts the memory search to information near the anchor.

Part B · Matlin & Farmer (pp. 463–472)
Lecture 16 of 43 · objectives J5

📏 Anchoring and confidence intervals

Why our ‘98% sure’ ranges miss so often

❓ This lecture answers: Why do the ranges we feel ‘98% sure’ about contain the true answer only about 60% of the time?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L15: anchoring on our best guess makes our ranges too narrow, which is one reason we are more confident than we should be.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · anchoring makes intervals too narrowBlock & Harper (1991); Hoffrage (2004): How often do ranges people feel 98% sure about actually contain the true answer?
  • SHOWS · misunderstanding confidence intervalsTeigen & Jorgensen (2005): How certain do people really feel about ranges they give as 90% intervals?
  • A confidence interval = the range within which you expect a number to fall a certain percentage of the time.
  • 98% intervals should contain the answer 98% of the time; they actually do only ≈60% of the time (Block & Harper, 1991; Hoffrage, 2004).
  • Mechanism: best estimate = anchor, then adjust up and down too little (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).
  • People also misunderstand intervals: students’ 90% intervals reflected only ≈50% certainty (Teigen & Jorgensen, 2005).
  • Fix: question your anchor and widen your range; ask what features of the situation should move you.
🪝 Memory hook: Your ‘98% sure’ is really ‘60% sure’: widen the net 🎣.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Confidence intervals are too narrow because adjustment from the anchor is too small: a form of overconfidence.
Tap to open ▸
Guess the number of students in your country with a range you are 98% sure about. Most people give a narrow band around their first guess, so if the first guess is off, the whole range misses.
Interval requestedExpected hit rateObservedSource
98%98%≈60%Block & Harper (1991); Hoffrage (2004)
90%90%≈50% certaintyTeigen & Jorgensen (2005)

How does anchoring explain narrow confidence intervals?

We use our best estimate as an anchor and adjust too little in both directions.

What fraction of 98% intervals actually contain the answer?

About 60%.

Part C · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501)
Lecture 17 of 43 · objectives D2 · D5

🎯 Bounded rationality and satisficing

Good enough beats perfect when time is short

❓ This lecture answers: Do people search for the best option, or do they pick the first one that is good enough?
↳ How it fits: This opens the choosing side: people are not perfect optimisers but rational within limits, and satisficing (‘good enough’) is often a smart response to those limits.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · satisficing under limited capacityChen & Sun (2003): Do people with a more limited working memory satisfice more often?
  • Classical decision theory assumed people optimise; from the 1950s researchers challenged this.
  • Bounded rationality (Simon, 1957): we are rational, but within limits; not irrational.
  • Satisficing: consider options one by one and pick the first that is good enough to meet your minimum level.
  • More satisficing when working memory is limited (Chen & Sun, 2003); also used where too much information hurts (choosing suppliers in e-markets).
  • Appropriateness depends on the situation: buying gum before catching a train ✓, diagnosing a disease ✗.
🪝 Memory hook: Satisfice = satisfy + suffice ✅.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Bounded rationality means making good-enough decisions within real limits.
Tap to open ▸
You need a birthday present in 20 minutes. You don’t compare every shop: the first decent present you find, you buy. That is satisficing, and it is often the smart choice.
Optimising (classical theory)Satisficing (Simon)

🧩 Comprehension check

What does bounded rationality mean?

People are rational, but within limits of time, resources and cognitive capacity.

When is satisficing a poor strategy?

For important decisions such as diagnosing a disease.

Part C · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501)
Lecture 18 of 43 · objectives D2 · D5

🔻 Elimination by aspects

Cutting a long list down, one attribute at a time

❓ This lecture answers: How do people cut a long list of options down to one, and what can go wrong when they do?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L17: elimination by aspects is another limited-rationality strategy that makes big choices manageable but can throw out an option that was best on a feature never checked.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · narrow first, then compare carefullyPayne (1976): How do people combine quick elimination and careful comparison when choosing among many options?
  • Used when there are more alternatives than we can consider in the time available (Tversky, 1972).
  • Focus on one aspect (cost), set a minimum criterion (under $20,000), eliminate options that fail (Stanford).
  • Pick a second aspect (West Coast), set a criterion, eliminate again … until a single option remains (Dawes, 2000).
  • Risk: aspects you never consider (car: maintenance, insurance) can matter more than the one you used.
  • Typical combination: EBA or satisficing to narrow the field, then careful strategies such as subjective expected utility for the last few (Payne, 1976).
🪝 Memory hook: EBA = a series of sieves: each aspect shakes out more options 🪣.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Elimination by aspects simplifies big choices, but can throw out an option that is excellent on an aspect you never checked.
Tap to open ▸
Choosing a flat online: ‘under €900’ (filter), ‘near campus’ (filter), ‘has a balcony’ (filter)… until one is left. You never compared all flats on everything.

Describe the steps of elimination by aspects.

How do people often combine EBA with other strategies?

Part C · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501)
Lecture 19 of 43 · objectives J2

🎲 Rules of probability and conditional probability

What statisticians calculate, and why we don’t

❓ This lecture answers: What probability rules would a statistician use, and why do we hardly ever use them in daily life?
↳ How it fits: This restates the theme’s contrast in its simplest form: exact rules like Bayes are hard to apply, so everyday judgement runs on shortcuts instead.
  • Statisticians use rules: probability of one of 10 equal candidates = 0.1.
  • Probability of not getting it = 1 − 0.1 = 0.9 (complement).
  • Probability that one of two roommates gets it = 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.2.
  • Conditional probability = likelihood of one event given another; calculated with Bayes’s theorem.
  • Bayes is complex, so people rarely use it in everyday reasoning, despite its importance for science and diagnosis; instead we use heuristics.
🪝 Memory hook: Not = 1 − p; Or = p + p; Given = Bayes.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Because exact calculation is hard, everyday probability judgement runs on heuristics.
Tap to open ▸
Probability rules are like grammar rules: everyone ‘knows’ them, but in conversation we speak by feel. In everyday judgement we go by feel too, and that feel is a heuristic.
QuestionCalculationAnswer

Lee does not1 − 0.10.9
Lee or the roommate0.1 + 0.10.2

What is conditional probability?

The probability of one event given that another has occurred.

Why don’t people use Bayes’s theorem in daily life?

It is complex to compute, so they rely on heuristics instead.

Part C · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501)
Lecture 20 of 43 · objectives J4 · J5

👶 The representativeness heuristic (Sternberg)

Birth orders, coins, birthdays and ‘man-who’ arguments

❓ This lecture answers: Why do some birth orders, coin sequences and anecdotes feel more likely than they are?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L4: the ‘looks typical’ shortcut also makes us expect randomness to look mixed, trust tiny samples and ‘man-who’ stories, and overlook base rates.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SHOWS · representativenessKahneman & Tversky (1972), birth orders: Do people judge a mixed-looking birth order as more common than an equally likely uneven one?
  • SHOWS · belief in small samplesTversky & Kahneman (1971): Do people expect small samples to look just like the whole population?
  • We judge probability by (1) how similar an event is to its population and (2) how well it reflects the process that generated it (e.g. randomness).
  • GBGBBG feels likelier than BGBBBB, but each order has probability (½)⁶: the best estimate for both is 72 families (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972).
  • We underestimate runs in random sequences (HTHHTH vs HHHHTH); in a group of 40, two share a birthday in 1 of 10 groups; in a group of 14 the odds are better than even of birthdays within a day of each other.
  • We wrongly believe small samples resemble the population (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971) and trust ‘man-who’ anecdotes (Nisbett & Ross, 1980).
  • We ignore base rates: a chest pain means something very different in a 10-year-old than in a 60-year-old. Base-rate use can be taught (Gigerenzer, 1996).
🪝 Memory hook: Looks random ≠ is more likely 🎲.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Representativeness swaps ‘how likely?’ for ‘how typical does it look?’
Tap to open ▸
Any specific series of six births is equally likely. ‘GBGBBG’ just looks more like what we expect from randomness, so it feels likelier.

Why do people think GBGBBG is more likely than BGBBBB?

It looks more representative of the population (3 girls, 3 boys) and more random.

What is a ‘man-who’ argument?

Refuting statistics with an anecdote about one person who doesn’t fit them.

Part C · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501)
Lecture 21 of 43 · objectives J2 · J4

🔤 The availability heuristic (Sternberg)

Letters, -ing words, chores and plane crashes

❓ This lecture answers: Why do we think words starting with R are more common, or that we do most of the housework?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L11: these classic studies show that ease of bringing examples to mind, not true frequency, drives the estimate, even when our ego is not involved.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · availabilityTversky & Kahneman (1973), letter R: Do people think more words start with R than have R as the third letter?
  • SUPPORTS · availabilityRoss & Sicoly (1979): Why do both partners think they do most of the household chores?
  • SUPPORTS · availabilityTversky & Kahneman (1983), -ing words: Do people estimate more 7-letter words ending in -ing than words with n second to last?
  • Availability: judge by how easily relevant instances come to mind (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973).
  • More English words have R in the third position than first, but first-letter words are easier to generate (same for K, L, N, V).
  • Ross & Sicoly (1979): each spouse claimed about 16 of 20 chores → 80% + 80% > 100%; also in basketball teams and lab tasks.
  • Not only self-serving: estimates for ‘_ _ _ _ i n g’ were more than twice those for ‘_ _ _ _ _ n _’, which logically can’t have fewer (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983).
  • We fear flying more than driving because plane crashes are always in the news.
🪝 Memory hook: What comes to mind first isn’t what happens most.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Ease of retrieval, not frequency, drives these judgements, even when no ego is involved.
Tap to open ▸
Both partners honestly think they do most of the housework: each remembers every time THEY did the dishes, but saw only some of the times the other did.

🧩 Comprehension check

Why did both spouses claim 80% of the chores?

Their own contributions were more available in memory.

Why is the -ing vs _n_ result a logical error?

Every 7-letter word ending in -ing has n as its second-to-last letter, so there can’t be more -ing words.

Part C · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501)
Lecture 22 of 43 · objectives D4

🖼️ Framing effects (Sternberg)

Same outcomes, different words, different choices

❓ This lecture answers: Why do people choose differently when the same outcomes are described as lives saved or as lives lost?
↳ How it fits: This shows that real choosers break a basic rule of the logical chooser: wording alone, gains versus losses, flips whether people play safe or gamble.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · framing effectTversky & Kahneman (1981), Asian disease problem: Does describing the same vaccines as lives saved or lives lost change which one people choose?
  • SUPPORTS · source credibility limits framingDruckman (2001): Does a frame still change opinions when it comes from a source with low credibility?
  • Framing effect: the way options are presented influences which option is selected (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981).
  • Potential gains → risk aversion: prefer a small certain gain to a larger uncertain one (Vaccine A).
  • Potential losses → risk seeking: prefer a large uncertain loss to a smaller certain one (Vaccine D).
  • Vaccines A and C have identical expected value; so do B and D: only the wording differs.
  • Framing matters in politics (a march framed as free speech vs public safety) but is weaker from low-credibility sources (Druckman, 2001).
🪝 Memory hook: Saved → play it safe 🛟; die → gamble 🎲.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Identical options framed as gains or losses produce opposite risk preferences.
Tap to open ▸
‘200 will be saved’ and ‘400 will die’ describe exactly the same result. But ‘saved’ makes you protect what you have, and ‘die’ makes you gamble to avoid the loss.
VaccineFrameOutcomeTypical choice
Again200 of 600 saved for sure✓ chosen (risk averse)
Bgain⅓ chance all saved, ⅔ nonerejected
Closs400 die for surerejected
Dloss⅓ chance nobody dies, ⅔ all die✓ chosen (risk seeking)

🧩 Comprehension check

Which vaccines have the same expected value?

A and C (both 200 live), and B and D.

What makes framing effects less persuasive?

A source with low credibility (Druckman, 2001).

Part C · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501)
Lecture 23 of 43 · objectives J5

😎 Biases: illusory correlation, overconfidence, hindsight

Seeing links, overrating ourselves, ‘knowing it all along’

❓ This lecture answers: Why do we see false links, overrate what we know, and feel we ‘knew it all along’ afterwards?
↳ How it fits: This gathers three biases the shortcuts feed, and shows why they matter: overconfidence and hindsight stop us learning from our own mistakes.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SHOWS · illusory correlationChapman & Chapman (1967-1975): Do clinicians see a link between big eyes in drawings and paranoia that does not exist?
  • SHOWS · overconfidenceFischhoff, Slovic & Lichtenstein (1977): When people feel 100% sure of a two-choice answer, how often are they actually right?
  • SHOWS · overconfidenceGrubb (2009): Do phone customers correctly predict how many minutes they will use each month?
  • SHOWS · hindsight bias hurts learningBiais & Weber (2009): Do investment bankers with strong hindsight bias perform worse, and does experience reduce it?
  • Illusory correlation: seeing events or attributes as going together when they don’t; fuels stereotypes; even in projective-test diagnoses (Chapman & Chapman).
  • Overconfidence: overvaluing one’s skills, knowledge or judgement; when 100% confident, people were right only 80% of the time (Fischhoff et al., 1977).
  • Reasons: not realising how little we know, unreliable sources, not wanting to think about being wrong; companies exploit it (phone contracts, Grubb, 2009).
  • Hindsight bias: after the fact, the signs seem obvious; people can’t predict study outcomes but find them ‘obvious’ afterwards.
  • Hindsight bias hinders learning: investment bankers with strong hindsight bias perform worse, and experience doesn’t reduce it.
🪝 Memory hook: Illusory link 🔗 · inflated self 🎈 · ‘I knew it’ 🔙.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Overconfidence and hindsight bias stop us from learning from our mistakes.
Tap to open ▸
When you’re 100% sure of a quiz answer, you’re wrong about one time in five. And once you hear an answer, you feel you knew it all along, so you never notice how often you were wrong.
BiasDefinitionStudy / example
Illusory correlationperceiving a relationship that doesn’t existbig eyes ↔ paranoia (Chapman & Chapman, 1967–1975)
Overconfidenceovervaluing one’s own skills, knowledge or judgement100% confident → 80% correct (Fischhoff et al., 1977); phone contracts (Grubb, 2009)
Hindsight biasbelieving afterwards that the outcome was predictableoutcomes of experiments ‘obvious’; bankers (Biais & Weber, 2009)

🧩 Comprehension check

What happened when people were 100% confident in Fischhoff et al. (1977)?

They were correct only about 80% of the time.

Why does hindsight bias hinder learning?

If you think you always expected the outcome, there is no gap between expectation and outcome to learn from.

Part C · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501)
Lecture 24 of 43 · objectives J5

🎰 Gambler’s fallacy and the hot hand

Two opposite mistakes about streaks

❓ This lecture answers: Why do some people think a win is ‘due’ after losses while others think a streak will continue?
↳ How it fits: This shows the ‘looks typical’ shortcut gone wrong in two opposite directions: both errors forget that independent events, like coin tosses, have no memory.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · hot hand is a fallacyGilovich, Vallone & Tversky (1985): After a few baskets in a row, does a player really score more often on the next shot?
  • Heuristics and fallacies are studied together: applying a heuristic can produce a fallacy.
  • Gambler’s fallacy: believing that a random event is influenced by earlier random events (‘after 5 losses I’m due to win’).
  • Each bet or coin toss is independent: equal chance on the 6th as on the 1st or the 1,001st.
  • It is the representativeness heuristic gone awry: we expect a short run to look like the long-run pattern.
  • Hot hand = the opposite belief: a streak will continue. Basketball records show no such effect (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985); defenders exploit the belief.
🪝 Memory hook: Coins have no memory 🪙.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Independent events have no memory: neither ‘due’ nor ‘hot’ changes the odds.
Tap to open ▸
A roulette wheel doesn’t know it landed on red five times. The gambler thinks black is ‘due’; the fan thinks red is ‘hot’. Both are seeing patterns in independent events.
Gambler’s fallacyHot-hand effect
Beliefthe run will END (due to change)the run will CONTINUE
Examplelost 5 bets → win is duemade a basket → next shot likelier
Realityindependent eventsno streak effect in records
Rootrepresentativenessperceived pattern in random runs

Simulate 10,000 fair coin flips. After every run of 5 heads, how often is the next flip heads?

How are the gambler’s fallacy and the hot hand opposites?

One expects a streak to reverse, the other expects it to continue.

Which heuristic underlies the gambler’s fallacy?

Representativeness: the expectation that a sequence should look representative of the random process.

Part C · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501)
Lecture 25 of 43 · objectives J5

❤️ The conjunction fallacy (Sternberg)

Heart attacks, -ing words and the power of frequencies

❓ This lecture answers: Why do people rate ‘over 55 and had a heart attack’ as likelier than ‘had a heart attack’, and how can wording fix it?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L4 and L10: the conjunction fallacy can come from either shortcut, and asking ‘how many out of 1,000’ makes it shrink sharply.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · frequency formats reduce conjunction fallacyTversky & Kahneman (1983), health survey: Do fewer people rate 'over 55 and heart attack' above 'heart attack' when asked in counts?
  • SUPPORTS · presentation format shapes reasoningGigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995): Does writing the same numbers as frequencies rather than percentages change how well people reason?
  • Conjunction fallacy: a higher estimate for a subset of events than for the larger set that contains it.
  • Availability can cause it (-ing vs _n_ words); so can representativeness (Linda).
  • Health survey: ‘had a heart attack’ estimated at 18%, ‘over 55 and had a heart attack’ at 30%; 65% gave the subset a higher estimate.
  • Rephrased as frequencies (‘how many of the 1,000 men…’), only 25% did.
  • Presentation format shapes whether people reason correctly (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995).
🪝 Memory hook: Percentages trick you; ‘how many out of 1,000’ saves you.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Frequency formats sharply reduce the conjunction fallacy.
Tap to open ▸
Out of 1,000 men, picture those with a heart attack. Now pick out those who are also over 55: obviously fewer. Thinking in counts makes the subset visible.
FormatMean: heart attackMean: over 55 AND heart attack% committing fallacy
Percentages18%30%65%
Frequencies (of 1,000 men)––25%
▶ conjunction fallacy frequencies▶ Gigerenzer frequency format(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why is 30% for ‘over 55 and heart attack’ impossible relative to 18%?

It is a subset of all men with a heart attack, so it must be ≤ 18%.

What reduced the fallacy?

Asking in frequencies (‘how many of 1,000 men’) instead of percentages.

Part C · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501)
Lecture 26 of 43 · objectives J5 · D2

💸 The sunk-cost fallacy

Throwing good money after bad

❓ This lecture answers: Why do we keep putting money or time into something just because we have already invested in it?
↳ How it fits: This shows a choosing error: a logical chooser looks only at future costs and benefits, while real people let money that is already gone steer them.
  • Sunk-cost fallacy: continuing to invest in something because you have already invested in it and hope to recover the investment.
  • Lemon car: after thousands in repairs you pay for another, to ‘justify’ past spending.
  • But the earlier money is already lost; more repairs won’t bring it back.
  • Miserable holiday: staying the second week to justify the cost, with no hope it improves.
  • Rational rule: judge only future costs and benefits; treat the past spending as sunk.
🪝 Memory hook: Sunk = gone. Decide from today forward ➡️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Past costs that can’t be recovered should not drive future decisions.
Tap to open ▸
If a film is terrible after 30 minutes, the ticket money is spent whether you stay or go. Staying only costs you another hour.
ExampleSunk costFallacious choiceRational choice
Lemon carthousands already spent on repairspay for another repairconsider a new car
Bad holidayholiday already paidstay the second weekgo home early
Ski trips (Robinson-Riegler)$100 vs $50 ticketsgo on the dearer tripgo on the more enjoyable trip
▶ sunk cost fallacy explained▶ sunk cost examples(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Define the sunk-cost fallacy.

Continuing to invest because of what you already invested, hoping to recover it.

What should a rational decision maker consider instead?

Only the future costs and benefits of each option.

Part C · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio (pp. 491–501)
Lecture 27 of 43 · objectives D2 · D5

🏃 Fast-and-frugal heuristics and take-the-best

The bright side of heuristics

❓ This lecture answers: Can simple shortcuts like ‘take the best’ reason lead to decisions as good as careful calculation?
↳ How it fits: This shows the bright side of the theme’s shortcuts: in the right environment, using little information quickly can match or beat complex strategies.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · take-the-best heuristicGigerenzer & Goldstein (1996): Can deciding on just the single best cue match more complex strategies that use all the information?
  • SHOWS · competence vs performance gapStanovich (2010): Do statistics experts and high scorers avoid the usual biases in everyday decisions?
  • Heuristics don’t always lead to errors (Cohen, 1981): we use them because they are so often right.
  • Take-the-best: decide on the single most important criterion; often as good as or better than complex strategies (Gigerenzer & Goldstein, 1996).
  • It belongs to the fast-and-frugal heuristics: little information, quick decisions, rationality within limits of time, information and capacity.
  • They describe sports decisions, lunch choices, doctors prescribing for depression and business decisions.
  • Competence vs performance: even experts and high scorers show biases in everyday life (Stanovich, 2010).
🪝 Memory hook: One good reason can beat ten mediocre ones 🥇.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Simple heuristics can produce excellent decisions in the right environment.
Tap to open ▸
Buying a car on safety alone sounds lazy, but if safety is what you care about most, it usually gives you a great choice without the headache.

Fast-and-frugal (class)little information, fast; bounded rationalityGigerenzer, Todd & ABC (1999)
Satisficingfirst good-enough optionSimon (1957)

What is the take-the-best heuristic?

Base the decision on the single most important criterion.

What does ‘competence vs performance’ mean here?

People may have the knowledge to reason well, yet still show biases in everyday decisions.

Part D · Matlin (pp. 436–446)
Lecture 28 of 43 · objectives D4

🎟️ The framing effect: background information

Lost tickets, lost bills and mental accounts

❓ This lecture answers: Why would you buy a new concert ticket after losing a €20 note, but not after losing the €20 ticket itself?
↳ How it fits: This shows framing through background context: we file money in mental accounts by topic, so the same €20 loss leads to different choices.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · mental accountingKahneman & Tversky (1984), lost ticket: Does it matter whether you lost the €20 ticket or a €20 note when deciding to buy a ticket?
  • The framing effect: the outcome of a decision depends on (1) the background context and (2) the wording of the question.
  • Matlin’s mail example: the same legislation described as ‘17 states’ or ‘33 states’ creates a very different emotional reaction.
  • Demonstration 12.7: if you lose your €20 ticket, only 46% would buy another; if you lose a €20 bill, 88% would buy a ticket.
  • We keep mental expense accounts by topic: a second ticket doubles the ‘concert account’; a lost bill is filed elsewhere.
  • A perfectly ‘rational’ decision maker would answer both problems the same: you are €20 poorer either way.
🪝 Memory hook: Same €20, different mental drawer 🗄️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The context in which a loss occurs changes how we decide, even when the money is the same.
Tap to open ▸
If you lose the ticket, paying again feels like paying €40 for one concert. If you lose a €20 note, it feels like bad luck that has nothing to do with the concert.
ProblemWhat was lost% who would pay €20Mental account
1the ticket46%concert account → concert now costs €40
2a €20 bill88%general money; concert still costs €20

🧩 Comprehension check

Why do fewer people buy a new ticket after losing the ticket?

They put both costs in the same ‘concert’ mental account, so the concert seems to cost €40.

What two factors does the framing effect involve, according to Matlin?

The background context of the choice and the wording of the question.

Part D · Matlin (pp. 436–446)
Lecture 29 of 43 · objectives D4

🗣️ The framing effect: wording and prospect theory

Lives saved vs lives lost

❓ This lecture answers: How does wording a choice as gains or as losses change our appetite for risk, and how does prospect theory explain it?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L22: the lives-saved versus lives-lost effect is large and robust, and prospect theory names the pattern: play safe with gains, gamble with losses.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · prospect theory framingTversky & Kahneman (1981), disease problem: Does wording a programme as lives saved or lives lost change whether people choose the risky one?
  • SUPPORTS · framing effect is robustMayhorn et al. (2002): Do older adults show the same gain and loss framing effect as younger people?
  • Survey designers know that the exact wording of a question changes answers (Bruine de Bruin, 2011).
  • ‘Saved’ wording: 72% chose the sure Program A (risk averse), 28% the risky B.
  • ‘Die’ wording: only 22% chose the sure Program C; 78% chose the risky D (risk seeking).
  • Identical deep structure; only the surface (saved vs lost) differs. Prospect theory: gains → avoid risks, losses → seek risks.
  • Robust: large effects, also in statistically sophisticated people; tip: reword your own decisions to check your choice.
🪝 Memory hook: Gain words 🛟 safe; loss words 🎲 gamble.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Describing the same outcome as a gain or a loss flips our attitude to risk.
Tap to open ▸
The doctors aren’t choosing different programmes; they hear different words. ‘200 saved’ sounds like a win to protect; ‘400 die’ sounds like a loss worth gambling to avoid.
ProgramWordingOutcome% choosing
Asaved200 saved for sure72%
Bsaved⅓: 600 saved; ⅔: none saved28%
Cdie400 die for sure22%
Ddie⅓: nobody dies; ⅔: 600 die78%

State the two predictions of prospect theory illustrated here.

Part D · Matlin (pp. 436–446)
Lecture 30 of 43 · objectives J5 · D2

🔮 Overconfidence about decisions

From trials to wars, and a crystal ball to fix it

❓ This lecture answers: How common and how costly is overconfidence in real decisions, and what can reduce it?
↳ How it fits: Answers part of ‘why are we so sure of ourselves’: people from students to politicians overrate their judgements, and arguing against yourself (the crystal ball) helps.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SHOWS · individual differences in overconfidenceStanovich (1999): What share of students are overconfident about their judgements, and how many are not?
  • SHOWS · cultural differences in overconfidenceYates (2010): Do people in China, the US and Japan differ in how overconfident they are?
  • SUPPORTS · crystal ball reduces overconfidenceCannon-Bowers & Salas (1998), crystal ball: Does imagining that your favourite explanation is wrong make you less overconfident?
  • Overconfidence: confidence in your judgements is higher than your actual performance warrants.
  • Already seen: illusory correlation (sure of a non-existent link) and anchoring (too-narrow confidence intervals).
  • Shown for predictions of survival, bankruptcies, trial verdicts; people overrate their social, creative, leadership and academic skills; scientists overrate their theories.
  • Individual and cultural differences: 77% of students overconfident, 23% not (Stanovich, 1999); China > US > Japan (Yates, 2010).
  • Politicians: overrate their chances of success and the accuracy of their data (Iraq). De-biasing: the crystal-ball technique.
🪝 Memory hook: If you’re sure, imagine the crystal ball says you’re wrong 🔮.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Overconfidence is common and costly; deliberately arguing against yourself reduces it.
Tap to open ▸
Most people believe they are above-average drivers. That can’t be true of most people, and the same thinking shows up in politics, business and exams.
AspectFinding
Domainspatient survival, bankruptcy, trial verdicts; own social, creative, leadership skills; scientific theories
Individual differences77% overconfident, 23% on target or underconfident (Stanovich, 1999)
CultureChina most, US intermediate, Japan least and slowest (Yates, 2010)
Politicsleaders overestimate success and data accuracy (Iraq, WMD)
Remedycrystal-ball technique: assume you are wrong and explain why

🧩 Comprehension check

What is the crystal-ball technique?

Imagine a perfect crystal ball shows your favoured hypothesis is wrong; then search for and support alternative explanations.

Which country was least overconfident in Yates (2010)?

Japan (they also took longest to decide).

Part D · Matlin (pp. 436–446)
Lecture 31 of 43 · objectives J5

⏳ The planning fallacy and reasons for overconfidence

Why your essay always takes longer

❓ This lecture answers: Why do we always underestimate how long a project will take, and what are the deeper reasons for overconfidence?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L30: the planning fallacy is overconfidence caused by an ideal scenario we anchor on and adjust too little, and breaking the task into steps helps.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SHOWS · planning fallacyBuehler et al. (2002): Do people correctly estimate how much time and money their projects will need?
  • SUPPORTS · debiasing the planning fallacyForsyth & Burt: Does splitting a project into parts and estimating each part give more accurate time estimates?
  • SUPPORTS · debiasing the planning fallacyBuehler (2012): Does imagining someone else doing the task, obstacles included, improve time estimates?
  • Planning fallacy: underestimating the time (or money) a project needs and expecting it to be easy; replicated in the US, Canada and Japan.
  • Causes: an optimistic scenario, remembering past tasks as quick, expecting more free time in future: anchoring with too little adjustment.
  • Fixes: break the project into parts; envision and rehearse each step; imagine another person doing it, obstacles included.
  • Five reasons for overconfidence: shaky knowledge, available confirming examples, forgetting other hypotheses, dismissing them, lack of public education.
  • My-side bias: overconfidence that your own view is correct in a confrontation; try to consider the other side.
🪝 Memory hook: Plan for the person you are, not the person you hope to be next Tuesday 📅.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Overconfidence in planning comes from an ideal scenario we never adjust enough.
Tap to open ▸
You think your paper takes 10 hours because you imagine the perfect week. Real weeks have interruptions; plan for those.
Reason for overconfidenceExplanation
1 shaky knowledgeunaware that knowledge rests on uncertain assumptions or unreliable sources
2 confirmationconfirming examples are available; we don’t search for counterexamples
3 memorywe can’t recall the other possible hypotheses
4 dismissaleven when recalled, alternatives seem trivial
5 educationpeople aren’t taught about overconfidence, so they don’t switch to Type 2
