🧩 Comprehension check

Give two strategies against the planning fallacy.

Divide the project into parts and estimate each; visualise another person doing it, including obstacles (also: rehearse each step).

What is my-side bias?

Overconfidence that your own view is correct in a confrontational situation.

Part D · Matlin (pp. 436–446)
Lecture 32 of 43 · objectives J5

🔙 The hindsight bias

‘I knew it all along’

❓ This lecture answers: Why do events seem so predictable once we know how they turned out?
↳ How it fits: This adds the last overconfidence bias: the known outcome acts like an anchor and quietly rewrites our memory of what we expected beforehand.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SHOWS · hindsight bias and memory reconstructionCarli (1999): Does knowing how a story ends change what people think they could have predicted and remember?
  • Hindsight bias: after an event, we judge it to have been inevitable; we ‘knew it all along’ (Hastie & Dawes, 2010).
  • It is overconfidence about what we could have predicted; we reconstruct the past to match the present.
  • Carli (1999): identical stories with a tragic or a happy ending; each group said it could have predicted its ending and falsely remembered ending-consistent details.
  • Helps explain blaming the victim; found in North America, Europe, Asia, Australia; in doctors, politics and business, though not always strong.
  • Explanations: the known outcome works as a 100% anchor; and we misremember the past to fit the outcome.
🪝 Memory hook: After the fact, every road looks like it led here 🛣️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Knowing the outcome rewrites our memory of how predictable it was.
Tap to open ▸
Once you know how the film ends, you spot the ‘clues’ everywhere and think the ending was obvious. Viewers who saw a different ending would find different clues just as obvious.
📄 Carli (1999)
ElementDetail
QuestionDoes knowing an outcome change what people think they could have predicted and remember?
MethodStudents read a story about Barbara and Jack with either a tragic or a happy (marriage proposal) ending, then took a true/false memory test including items never mentioned.
FindingsBoth groups said they could have predicted their ending and falsely recognised details consistent with it.
ConclusionHindsight bias distorts both predictions and memory.
Why it mattersExplains victim blaming; shows reconstruction of the past.

🧩 Comprehension check

What are two explanations for the hindsight bias?

Anchoring on the known (100%) outcome with too little adjustment, and misremembering the past to fit the outcome.

Why is Carli’s study important socially?

It helps explain why people ‘blame the victim’ after a tragic event.

Part D · Matlin (pp. 436–446)
Lecture 33 of 43 · objectives D2 · D3 · D5

🌿 Current status: ecological rationality and defaults

Kahneman vs Gigerenzer

❓ This lecture answers: Are heuristics mainly sources of error, or smart tools fitted to our real environment, as Gigerenzer argues?
↳ How it fits: This gives a second answer to the theme’s question: shortcuts often serve us well in natural settings, and changing the setting, such as the default option, changes the choice.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • SUPPORTS · default heuristic; ecological rationalityGigerenzer (2008), organ donors: Why are almost all French people organ donors but only 28% of Americans?
  • SUPPORTS · heuristics usually serve us wellHarris et al. (2009): Are people's judgements about future events as unrealistic as the heuristics approach suggests?
  • Some argue the heuristics approach underestimates people: e.g. fairly realistic judgements about future events (Harris et al., 2009).
  • Gigerenzer: people do well when given a fair chance, in naturalistic settings and with frequencies rather than probabilities.
  • Ecological rationality (Todd & Gigerenzer, 2007): we create varied heuristics that make useful, adaptive decisions in our real environment.
  • Default heuristic: choose the standard option. US (opt-in) organ donors 28% vs France (opt-out) 99.9%.
  • Lab tasks sometimes contradict our real-world knowledge (Linda would be a feminist); both approaches agree heuristics usually serve us well.
🪝 Memory hook: Change the default, change the decision 🔁.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Heuristics are adapted to environments; designing the environment (defaults) changes the decision.
Tap to open ▸
Most people never fill in the organ-donor form. Where ‘donor’ is the default, almost everyone is a donor; where you must opt in, few are. Same lazy rule, completely different outcome.
Kahneman & TverskyGigerenzer

Explain the organ-donor difference with one heuristic.

The default heuristic: people keep the standard option, opt-in in the US (28% donors) vs opt-out in France (99.9%).

What is ecological rationality?

Using heuristics that fit the structure of the real environment, giving adaptive decisions.

Part E · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 481–489)
Lecture 34 of 43 · objectives J5 · D1

🎉 From judgement to decision under risk

Spotlight effect, miscalibration and why choice brings risk

❓ This lecture answers: How do judgements feed into decisions, and why does making a choice bring risk with it?
↳ How it fits: This bridges the two halves of the theme: judgements are the raw material for decisions, and choosing then adds uncertainty, which leads to the ideal-versus-real chooser comparison.
  • Judgement recap: anchoring underlies the spotlight effect (we think others notice us more than they do).
  • Hindsight bias: after the fact we inflate how well we knew it would happen; miscalibration: confidence is a poor indicator of accuracy.
  • Judgements form the ‘database’ for decisions: ‘Will Tom be at the party?’ → ‘pretty sure’ → ‘let’s go’.
  • Decision-making adds a choice between alternatives, and with it risk/uncertainty: your choice could be wrong.
  • Two approaches follow: normative (how an ideal chooser should decide) and descriptive (how people actually decide).
🪝 Memory hook: Judge the odds 🎲 → choose the option 🔀 → live with the risk ⚠️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Decisions build on judgements and add choice under uncertainty.
Tap to open ▸
Whether you go to the party depends on how likely you think Tom is to be there. Your judgement feeds your decision, and any decision can turn out wrong.
TermMeaning
Spotlight effectbelieving others notice our actions and appearance more than they do (anchoring on our own view)
Hindsight biasinflating, after an event, how much we knew it would happen
Miscalibration of confidenceour confidence is not a good indicator of accuracy
Riskthe chance that the chosen alternative is the wrong one

Which heuristic underlies the spotlight effect?

Anchoring and adjustment.

What does decision-making add to judgement?

A choice between alternatives, which introduces risk or uncertainty.

Part E · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 481–489)
Lecture 35 of 43 · objectives D1 · D3

🪙 Expected utility theory

How an ideal decision maker should choose

❓ This lecture answers: How would a perfectly rational decision maker choose between risky options, according to expected utility theory?
↳ How it fits: This sets the ideal chooser’s rule (value times chance) and its key principle of invariance, the yardstick against which real choices are judged next.
  • Expected utility theory: under uncertainty we decide on two factors: the utility of outcomes and their probability.
  • Utility = whatever end a person wants (happiness, money…); Baron (1999): think of it as the ‘good’ a decision produces.
  • Coin: heads → $40 (½ × 40 = $20) vs die: a 4 → $50 (⅙ × 50 ≈ $8.33): most choose the coin.
  • It is a normative model: how perfectly rational people would choose, a baseline for real behaviour.
  • Key normative principle: invariance: preferences must not depend on how choices are presented.
🪝 Memory hook: EU = value × chance ✖️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Expected utility tells us how we should choose; it is the yardstick for rational decisions.
Tap to open ▸
A 50% chance at €40 is worth about €20 to you on average; a one-in-six chance at €50 is worth only about €8. The ideal chooser always takes the bigger product.

What two factors does expected utility theory combine?

The utility (value, ‘good’) of each outcome and its probability.

Why is expected utility called normative?

It describes how a perfectly rational decision maker should choose.

🔄 Invariance and preference reversals

Choosing one gamble but pricing the other higher

❓ This lecture answers: Why do people pick one gamble but put a higher price on the other, and what does that say about rational choice?
↳ How it fits: Here the ideal chooser fails its first test: preference reversals break invariance, so expected utility does not describe how people really choose.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • AGAINST · expected utility (invariance)Lichtenstein & Slovic (1971, 1973): Is the gamble people choose to play also the one they would put the higher price on?
  • Invariance: if I prefer A over B in one situation, I should prefer A in another as long as A and B are identical.
  • People easily violate it: they switch preferences based only on presentation.
  • Preference reversals (Lichtenstein & Slovic, 1971): the gamble chosen depends on the probability of winning; the selling price depends on the amount to win.
  • Same in a Las Vegas casino with real gamblers and card dealers (1973).
  • So expected utility is a poor descriptive model: we lack full information, can’t combine it well, can’t foresee consequences.
🪝 Memory hook: Pick by odds 🎯, price by prize 💰 = inconsistent.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Preference reversals show that preferences depend on how the question is asked.
Tap to open ▸
Asked which bet you’d play, you pick the safe one. Asked what each bet is worth, you put a higher price on the long shot. A consistent person can’t do both.

Part E · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 481–489)
Lecture 37 of 43 · objectives D2 · D3

📈 Prospect theory: the value function

A descriptive model of how we really value outcomes

❓ This lecture answers: How do people really value gains and losses, according to the value function of prospect theory?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L36: prospect theory replaces the ideal model with a real one, where we measure outcomes from a reference point and losses hurt more than equal gains please.
  • Prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979): a descriptive model of why decisions violate expected utility.
  • We value outcomes as gains or losses from a reference point (what we have now), not as absolute end states.
  • Gains and losses are on different scales: the curve for losses is steeper: losing $50 hurts more than gaining $50 pleases (loss aversion).
  • Value grows ever more slowly with bigger gains (concave) → risk aversion for gains; convex for losses → risk seeking for losses.
  • Because preferences depend on the reference point, changing the frame changes the decision.
🪝 Memory hook: Losses loom larger than gains 📉 > 📈.
★ KEY INSIGHT · We judge outcomes as changes from a reference point, and losses weigh more than equal gains.
Tap to open ▸
Finding €50 is nice; losing €50 ruins your day. That imbalance, measured from what you have right now, is the heart of prospect theory.
FeatureMeaningConsequence
Reference pointvalue = change from what you have nowreframing shifts the reference point
Concave for gainseach extra unit of gain adds less valueprefer a sure gain (risk averse)
Convex for losseseach extra unit of loss hurts lessgamble to avoid a sure loss (risk seeking)
Steeper for losseslosses hurt more than equal gains pleaseloss aversion

What is the reference point in prospect theory?

What you have right now; outcomes are valued as gains or losses relative to it.

Why does the value function predict risk aversion for gains?

It is concave for gains: a sure gain is valued more than a gamble with the same expected value.

  • Framing affects medical decisions, health behaviour and decisions about continuing relationships.

⏳ Temporal value asymmetry

The future is worth more than the past

❓ This lecture answers: Do we value the same experience differently when it lies ahead of us rather than behind us?
↳ How it fits: This adds a time twist to prospect theory: future gains and losses feel bigger than equal past ones, so when an outcome happens also shapes how we value it.
🔬 Studies on this screen: the question each one asks, and what it means for the idea
  • AGAINST · prospect theory's single moment in timeCaruso, Gilbert & Wilson (2008): Do people value a winter-break trip more before it happens than after it is over?
  • Prospect theory’s asymmetry is gains vs losses; Caruso, Gilbert & Wilson (2008) add an asymmetry in time.
  • People place more value on future events than on equivalent past events (Seneca’s death argument feels wrong).
  • Winter-break study: before the break, trips were rated more enjoyable and people would pay $113 to extend them, vs $91 after the break.
  • Found in all five studies; the future is less certain and more changeable, so (rationally) valued more.
  • Implication: the pleasure or pain of gains and losses depends on whether they are past or still to come.
🪝 Memory hook: Ahead feels bigger than behind ⏩.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The same outcome is valued more when it lies in the future than in the past.
Tap to open ▸
A holiday you are looking forward to is worth more to you than the same holiday you have just had. Anticipation adds value; memory doesn’t.

🧾 Psychological accounting and sunk costs

❓ This lecture answers: Why do lost tickets and already-paid trips make us treat the same money differently?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L28 and L26: mental accounts and sunk costs show again that real choosers label money in their heads, while the ideal chooser treats a euro as a euro.

Part E · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 481–489)
Lecture 43 of 43 · objectives D2 · D3

🧰 Biases or adaptive tools?

Half-empty vs half-full, and how to decide better

❓ This lecture answers: Should we see heuristics as flaws in our thinking or as adaptive tools, and how can we decide better?
↳ How it fits: This closes the theme: whether shortcuts look like errors or smart tools depends on the environment, and knowing both views helps us make better decisions.
  • The Kahneman & Tversky programme asks why judgement falls short: emphasis on error and limitation.
  • Gigerenzer asks how we decide well despite limits: heuristics are an evolved adaptive toolbox, fast and frugal, shaped by mind and environment (ecological approach).
  • KT scenarios may lack ecological validity: specific, sometimes obscurely worded verbal problems.
  • Four misconceptions: heuristics give second-best results; are only for cognitive limits; only for minor decisions; more information is always better.
  • Everyone wants better decisions: errors are costly (2008 mortgage crisis) and the world grows more complex (Milkman et al., 2009).
🪝 Memory hook: Same glass, two views: errors 🥛 or tools 🧰.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Heuristics can be seen as sources of bias or as adaptive tools; their success depends on the environment.

🧩 Comprehension check

What is Gigerenzer’s ‘adaptive toolbox’?

An evolved set of fast-and-frugal heuristics fitted to the demands of real environments.

Name two misconceptions about heuristics according to Gigerenzer.

That heuristics give only second-best results, and that more information and computation are always better (also: only for limits, only minor decisions).

🧵 Synthesis

One thread runs through Theme 6: people replace hard questions with easy ones. Instead of ‘what is the probability?’ we ask ‘is it typical?’ (representativeness), ‘can I think of examples?’ (availability), ‘what number did I start from?’ (anchoring) or ‘how do I feel?’ (affect). Instead of ‘what is the best option?’ we ask ‘is this good enough?’ (satisficing) or ‘does it pass this one cut-off?’ (elimination by aspects). And instead of valuing final outcomes we ask ‘is this a gain or a loss from where I am?’ (prospect theory).

These substitutions are usually adaptive (Gigerenzer’s fast-and-frugal view), but they ignore information, so they fail predictably (Kahneman and Tversky’s biases): base rates, sample size and the conjunction rule disappear, memory distorts frequency, anchors stick, and the frame flips choices. Exam tip: for every bias, name the heuristic behind it, the information it ignores, a classic study with a number, and a fix (natural frequencies, the 2 × 2 table, reframing, considering alternatives).

Learning objectives A–C · Judgment
🎯 Learning objective · J1
❓ The question this screen answers
J1
How do people make judgments?

🧭 In plain words: Define judgment, contrast how we should judge (Bayes) with how we actually judge (heuristics), and say why heuristics exist.

  • Judgment = probability estimate under uncertainty
  • Normative: Bayes (prior odds × likelihood ratio)
  • Actual: heuristics (representativeness, availability, anchoring, affect)
  • Heuristics save effort; usually accurate
  • Bounded rationality; Type 1 vs Type 2
🪝 Memory hook: Bayes is the recipe; heuristics are tasting the soup.
★ KEY INSIGHT · People are not bad statisticians because they are stupid, but because they don’t calculate at all: they substitute an easier question (‘is this typical?’, ‘can I think of examples?’).
Tap to open ▸

Judgment is assessing the likelihood of an event using incomplete information, for example judging your chance of passing an exam from your past results. What matters in judgment is accuracy (Eysenck & Keane). Judgment is often the first stage of decision making.

How we should judge. Normatively, beliefs should be updated with Bayes’ theorem: the posterior odds of two hypotheses equal the prior odds (base rates) multiplied by the likelihood ratio (how probable the evidence is under each hypothesis). In the taxi-cab problem (85% Green, 15% Blue cabs; a witness who is right 80% of the time says ‘Blue’), the correct answer is (.15 × .80) : (.85 × .20) = 12 : 17, so a 41% chance the cab was Blue.

How we actually judge. Most people answer 80%. Tversky and Kahneman argued that people use heuristics: ‘strategies that ignore part of the information, with the goal of making decisions more quickly, frugally and/or accurately than more complex methods’ (Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier, 2011). The main ones are representativeness (judging by similarity), availability (judging by ease of retrieval) and anchoring-and-adjustment (starting from a number and adjusting too little). We also use the affect heuristic (judging by our feelings of dread or liking).

Why heuristics? They reduce cognitive effort and are usually accurate (Matlin). They fit bounded rationality (Simon, 1957): we are rational, but within the limits of our time, information and working memory. Gigerenzer adds that heuristics form an adaptive toolbox, fast-and-frugal tools tuned to real environments. In Kahneman’s terms, these quick judgments are Type 1 processing; slower, deliberate Type 2 processing can sometimes override them (e.g., Oppenheimer, 2004).

  • Listing heuristics without defining judgment.
  • Forgetting the normative benchmark (Bayes, base rates).
  • Presenting heuristics as always wrong.

Learning objectives A–C · Judgment
🎯 Learning objective · J2
❓ The question this screen answers
J2
How do people assess/estimate probabilities?

🧭 In plain words: Explain the probability rules people should use and the shortcuts they do use, with the classic demonstrations and the frequency-format finding.

  • Rules: complement, addition, conjunction, Bayes
  • People: representativeness, availability, anchoring, affect
  • Frequencies beat probabilities (16% → 46%)
  • Causal stories help base-rate use (43% → 8% neglect)
  • Motivation changes base-rate use (Ditto et al., 1998)
🪝 Memory hook: Your brain counts apples, not percentages of apples.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Our probability sense is poor with percentages but much better with counts of cases: ‘10 out of 1,000’ beats ‘1%’.
Tap to open ▸

The rules. Sternberg et al. (Table 12.1) list basic probability rules: the probability of one of 10 candidates winning is .1; of not winning, 1 − .1 = .9; of one of two people winning, .1 + .1 = .2. A conjunction of two events can never be more probable than either event alone. Conditional probability (the likelihood of one event given another) is computed with Bayes’ theorem, which combines base rates with the evidence.

What people do. Instead of applying these rules, people estimate probability by: (1) representativeness: how similar an outcome is to its population or to a random process (a family’s birth order G B G B B G ‘looks’ more likely than B G B B B B, although both are (1/2)⁶ = 1/64); (2) availability: how easily examples come to mind (more words seem to start with R than have R third, although the reverse is true; Tversky & Kahneman, 1973); (3) anchoring and adjustment: estimating 8×7×6×…×1 gives a median of 2,250 but 1×2×3×…×8 gives 512 (correct: 40,320); and (4) affect: risks that evoke more dread are judged more frequent (Pachur et al., 2012).

The format matters. People are much better with natural frequencies than with probabilities (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995): on a mammogram problem only 16% were correct with probabilities but 46% with frequencies. A meta-analysis confirmed the advantage (McDowell & Jacobs, 2017), and advanced medical students solved 45% of frequency problems vs 7% of probability problems (Hoffrage et al., 2015). The conjunction fallacy also dropped from 65% to 25% when the heart-attack question was asked as ‘how many of 1,000 men’ (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983). People also use base rates when the causal structure is clear (faded-paint taxi problem: base-rate neglect fell from 43% to 8%; Krynski & Tenenbaum, 2007) or when they are motivated to (Ditto et al., 1998).

  • Only describing heuristics, not the probability rules.
  • Forgetting the natural-frequency evidence.
  • Getting the multiplication-anchor numbers wrong.

Learning objectives A–C · Judgment
🎯 Learning objective · J3
❓ The question this screen answers
J3
Where do judgments go wrong? How are they biased?

🧭 In plain words: Name the situations in which heuristics misfire and the systematic biases that result, and add the critique that ‘biases’ are partly a lab artefact.

  • Cue not correlated with true probability → error
  • Representativeness: base rates, sample size, conjunctions
  • Availability: recency, familiarity, media
  • Anchoring: arbitrary anchors, small adjustments
  • Critique: biased samples, artificial tasks
🪝 Memory hook: A sat-nav that is great in your city but drives you into a lake abroad.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A bias is a heuristic used outside the environment where it works.
Tap to open ▸

Heuristics go wrong when the cue they rely on is not correlated with the true probability. Representativeness misfires when we ignore base rates (lawyer–engineer problem: Jack was judged .90 likely to be an engineer whether engineers were 70% or 30% of the sample; Kahneman & Tversky, 1973), ignore sample size (small samples are assumed to resemble the population; ‘man-who’ arguments), or violate the conjunction rule (Linda). Availability misfires when ease of recall is boosted by recency or familiarity and media coverage (Matlin, Figure 12.2): murders are judged more common than suicides (Lichtenstein et al., 1978); El Salvador and Indonesia were given similar populations although Indonesia’s was about 35 times larger (Brown & Siegler, 1992). Anchoring misfires when the anchor is arbitrary: experienced judges gave 28 months after a novice ‘prosecutor’ demanded 12, but 36 months after a demand of 34 (Englich & Mussweiler, 2001).

These produce systematic biases: overconfidence (people 100% sure were right only 80% of the time; Fischhoff et al., 1977; 98% confidence intervals contain the answer only about 60% of the time), hindsight bias (‘I knew it all along’; Carli, 1999), illusory correlation (Chapman & Chapman, 1969), the planning fallacy, confirmation and my-side bias, and in medicine anchoring, omission bias and overconfidence, linked to 36–77% of diagnostic errors (Saposnik et al., 2016; Croskerry, 2018). Emotion and motivation also bias judgments (Ditto et al., 1998; Lench & Darbor, 2014).

Critique. Eysenck and Keane note that heuristics are vaguely defined, theory is limited, and errors are not always due to biased processing: often we receive a biased sample of information (skin cancer is judged a more common cause of death than mouth and throat cancer because of media coverage; Hertwig et al., 2005), and lab tasks are artificial. Gigerenzer argues that heuristics are ecologically rational in real environments.

HeuristicRelies onGoes wrong when…Resulting error
RepresentativenessSimilarity / typicalityBase rate or sample size matterBase-rate neglect, conjunction fallacy, gambler’s fallacy
AvailabilityEase of recallRecency, familiarity, media distort recallMisjudged risks, illusory correlation
AnchoringA starting numberAnchor is arbitrary or wrongToo-narrow intervals, hindsight bias, planning fallacy
AffectFeelings (dread)Feelings ≠ frequencyOver-estimated dreaded risks
  • Listing biases without linking them to a heuristic.
  • No evidence/numbers.
  • No critique (environment, lab artificiality).

Learning objectives A–C · Judgment
🎯 Learning objective · J4
❓ The question this screen answers

Which heuristics do people use?

🧭 In plain words: Give a clear inventory of the heuristics in the readings, each with a definition and a classic example.

  • Representativeness, availability, anchoring, affect
