  • Take-the-best, default heuristic (fast & frugal)
  • Similarity → representativeness; examples → availability
🪝 Memory hook: R-A-A-A: Resemble, Available, Anchor, Affect.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Judgment heuristics answer ‘how likely?’; choice heuristics answer ‘which one?’.
Tap to open ▸
  • Representativeness: judging probability by how similar something is to its category or to the process that produced it (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972). Example: Linda; birth orders; Jack the ‘engineer’.
  • Availability: estimating frequency by how easily examples come to mind (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973). Example: words starting with R; spouses’ household chores (Ross & Sicoly, 1979).
  • Recognition heuristic (a special case of availability): if you recognise one of two options, infer it scores higher (Milan vs Modena; Goldstein & Gigerenzer, 2002). Usually accurate.
  • Anchoring and adjustment: start from an anchor and adjust insufficiently (8×7×… vs 1×2×…; roulette-wheel anchors for African UN countries).
  • Affect heuristic: using feelings (dread, liking) to judge risks and benefits (Pachur et al., 2012; Scherer et al., 2018).
  • Decision heuristics (Sternberg et al.): satisficing (take the first option that is good enough; Simon, 1957), elimination by aspects (drop options that fail a criterion, one attribute at a time; Tversky, 1972), take-the-best and other fast-and-frugal heuristics (Gigerenzer), and the default heuristic (stick with the option that happens if you do nothing: 28% organ donors in the US vs 99.9% in France; Gigerenzer, 2008).

Matlin’s tip for telling the first two apart: if the problem asks about similarity, it is representativeness; if it requires you to remember examples, it is availability.

  • Confusing representativeness with availability.
  • Leaving out the decision heuristics (satisficing, EBA).
  • No example per heuristic.

Learning objectives A–C · Judgment
🎯 Learning objective · J5
❓ The question this screen answers
J5
What are common biases and fallacies?

🧭 In plain words: Define each common bias/fallacy, give an example, and name the heuristic it comes from.

  • Representativeness → base-rate neglect, conjunction, gambler’s, hot hand
  • Availability → illusory correlation, risk misjudgment
  • Anchoring → overconfidence, hindsight, planning fallacy
  • Motivated: confirmation / my-side bias
  • Decision: sunk cost, framing
🪝 Memory hook: Gambler says ‘it must change’, hot hand says ‘it must continue’: both think chance has a memory.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Learn biases as a family tree: if you know the parent heuristic, you can explain the child bias.
Tap to open ▸
  • Base-rate neglect: ignoring how common something is (taxi-cab, lawyer–engineer). From representativeness.
  • Conjunction fallacy: judging A-and-B more likely than A (Linda; ‘spilling hot coffee’ vs ‘spilling coffee’). Double conjunction fallacy: A-and-B judged more likely than A and than B (49% of medical experts; Crupi et al., 2018).
  • Gambler’s fallacy: believing a random outcome is ‘due’ after a run (after five losses a win feels likely). Hot-hand effect: believing a streak will continue (basketball shooting; Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985). Both from representativeness.
  • Illusory correlation: seeing a relationship that is not there, by attending to one cell of the 2 × 2 table (Chapman & Chapman, 1969). From availability.
  • Overconfidence: confidence higher than accuracy (100% sure, 80% right), including too-narrow confidence intervals and the planning fallacy. Linked to anchoring.
  • Hindsight bias: after the outcome, believing you knew it all along (Carli, 1999). Linked to anchoring on the 100% known outcome.
  • Confirmation bias / my-side bias and belief bias: favouring information that fits what you already believe.
  • Sunk-cost fallacy: continuing because you already invested (ski trips: Arkes & Blumer, 1985).
  • In medicine: anchoring on the first symptom, omission bias (preferring inaction), overconfidence.
  • Mixing up gambler’s fallacy and hot hand.
  • Not giving the heuristic source.
  • Vague definitions without an example.

Learning objectives D–E · Decision making
🎯 Learning objective · D1
❓ The question this screen answers
D1
How should rational people make decisions?

🧭 In plain words: Describe the normative model: expected utility theory and its key principle of invariance.

  • Decision = choice under risk
  • Expected utility = utility × probability
  • Normative model = the ideal baseline
  • Invariance: description shouldn’t matter
  • Rational chooser optimises
🪝 Memory hook: $40 at 50% beats $50 at 17%: the rational chooser does the multiplication.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Normative models are a ruler: not a description of people, but the standard we measure them against.
Tap to open ▸

Decision making means choosing among alternatives, which always involves risk or uncertainty (Robinson-Riegler). The best-established normative model is expected utility theory: when facing an uncertain choice, a rational person weighs the utility of each outcome (the amount of ‘good’ it brings: happiness, money, etc.) by its probability, and chooses the option with the best combination. Example: ‘flip a coin, heads wins $40’ (expected value $20) vs ‘roll a die, a 4 wins $50’ (about $8.33): the first is the better choice even though the prize is smaller.

Expected utility theory is normative: it describes how a perfectly rational decision maker would choose, and serves as a baseline to compare real decisions with. One of its key principles is invariance: preferences should not depend on how the options are presented. If you prefer A to B in one description, you should prefer A to B in any equivalent description.

Classical decision theory also assumed decision makers are fully informed, infinitely sensitive to differences between options, and rational (Sternberg et al. describe how this ‘unlimited rationality’ was challenged). The rational decision maker optimises.

  • Defining utility only as money.
  • Forgetting invariance.
  • Calling expected utility descriptive.

Learning objectives D–E · Decision making
🎯 Learning objective · D2
❓ The question this screen answers
D2
How do people actually make decisions?

🧭 In plain words: Describe the descriptive picture: bounded rationality and choice heuristics, prospect theory, framing, mental accounting, sunk costs, emotion and overconfidence.

  • Bounded rationality: satisficing, elimination by aspects
  • Prospect theory: gains/losses vs reference point
  • Framing: risk averse (gains) vs risk seeking (losses)
  • Mental accounting & sunk costs
  • Emotion, stress, touch, overconfidence, defaults
🪝 Memory hook: You don’t buy the best phone; you buy the first one that ticks your boxes, and you keep it because you paid so much.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Real decisions are relative (to a reference point), lazy (good enough) and emotional.
Tap to open ▸

Bounded rationality (Simon, 1957): people are rational within limits of time, information and working memory, so they often satisfice (pick the first good-enough option) rather than optimise, or use elimination by aspects (Tversky, 1972), often narrowing options this way before comparing the last few carefully (Payne, 1976).

Prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979): we evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, and losses weigh more than gains. Hence framing effects: in a gain frame people are risk averse (72% choose the sure ‘200 saved’), in a loss frame risk seeking (78% choose the gamble over ‘400 die’; Tversky & Kahneman, 1981). Preference reversals also show inconsistency (Lichtenstein & Slovic, 1971, 1973, even in a Las Vegas casino).

Mental (psychological) accounting: losing a ticket feels different from losing the same amount of cash (46% vs 88% would buy a ticket). Sunk costs: we continue because of past investment (Michigan vs Wisconsin ski trip; Arkes & Blumer, 1985).

Emotion: acute stress (cold-pressor task) strengthens framing effects, because it increases reliance on System 1 (Porcelli & Delgado, 2009); a female experimenter’s touch on the shoulder increased financial risk taking (Levav & Argo, 2010). People also show overconfidence and the planning fallacy, use defaults (organ donation), and value the future more than the past (Caruso et al., 2008).

Gigerenzer adds that these heuristics are often ecologically rational: fast-and-frugal tools (take-the-best) that work well in real environments.

  • Only discussing framing.
  • No numbers for the Asian disease problem.
  • Forgetting bounded rationality/satisficing.

Learning objectives D–E · Decision making
🎯 Learning objective · D3
❓ The question this screen answers
D3
How do normative and descriptive decision making differ?

🧭 In plain words: Contrast the two approaches on goal, assumptions and evidence, and mention the debate about whether deviations are ‘irrational’.

  • Normative = should; descriptive = do
  • Absolute outcomes vs reference-point changes
  • Invariance vs framing effects
  • Optimising vs satisficing
  • Kahneman & Tversky (errors) vs Gigerenzer (adaptive)
🪝 Memory hook: The normative model is the GPS route; the descriptive model is the way you actually drive home.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The gap between the two is the research topic: every violation of expected utility is a clue about how the mind really works.
Tap to open ▸

Normative models (expected utility theory) prescribe how an ideal, fully rational decision maker should choose: weigh utilities by probabilities, optimise, and keep preferences invariant across descriptions. Descriptive models (prospect theory, bounded rationality, satisficing, elimination by aspects) describe how people actually choose.

They differ in assumptions: expected utility assumes we have all the information and can combine it perfectly, and that we can foresee consequences; Robinson-Riegler notes we rarely have all the information, cannot combine it accurately, and cannot foresee outcomes with certainty. Prospect theory replaces absolute final wealth with changes from a reference point, and gives losses more weight than gains.

The evidence for the difference is the violations of normative principles: framing effects and preference reversals violate invariance; sunk-cost and mental accounting violate the idea that only future consequences matter.

Interpretation differs. The Kahneman and Tversky programme asks why judgment falls short of optimisation (errors, illusions). Gigerenzer asks how we manage to make good decisions despite limitations: heuristics are an adaptive toolbox, and many ‘biases’ come from ecologically invalid, oddly worded lab scenarios. Both agree heuristics generally serve us well and that knowing their limits makes us better decision makers.

Normative (expected utility)Descriptive (prospect theory, bounded rationality)
QuestionHow should we choose?How do we choose?
Outcomes valued asFinal states (absolute)Gains/losses from a reference point
Losses vs gainsSymmetricLosses loom larger
Description of optionsIrrelevant (invariance)Matters (framing)
StrategyOptimiseSatisfice, eliminate by aspects, heuristics
  • Only defining the two terms without an example.
  • Not naming invariance as the violated principle.
  • Treating descriptive as ‘wrong’ without the Gigerenzer view.

Learning objectives D–E · Decision making
🎯 Learning objective · D4
❓ The question this screen answers
D4
How does the phrasing of a problem determine your decision?

🧭 In plain words: Explain framing: the same options described as gains vs losses lead to different choices; also background context (mental accounting).

  • Same outcomes, different description → different choice
  • Gain frame: risk averse (72% sure option)
  • Loss frame: risk seeking (78% gamble)
  • Background context: lost ticket vs lost cash (46% vs 88%)
  • Explained by reference point in prospect theory
🪝 Memory hook: ‘90% fat-free’ sells; ‘10% fat’ doesn’t.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Words move the reference point; the reference point decides whether an outcome feels like a gain or a loss.
Tap to open ▸

A framing effect occurs when the way options are presented influences the choice, even though the outcomes are identical (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981). Matlin distinguishes two factors: (1) the background context of the choice and (2) the wording of the question.

Wording. In the Asian disease problem, ‘200 people will be saved’ (sure) vs ‘1/3 chance 600 saved’ (risky) led 72% to choose the sure option; the identical choice phrased as ‘400 people will die’ vs ‘1/3 chance nobody dies’ led 78% to choose the risky option. A gain frame makes people risk averse; a loss frame makes them risk seeking. This follows from prospect theory: the frame shifts the reference point, so the same outcome is coded as a gain or as a loss.

Background context. People who lose a €20 ticket are less willing to buy another (46%) than people who lose a €20 note (88%), because the ticket loss is charged to the ‘concert account’ (psychological accounting; Kahneman & Tversky, 1984).

Framing is robust (also in statistically sophisticated people, young and older adults), appears in medical, health and relationship decisions, and is stronger under stress (Porcelli & Delgado, 2009). fMRI shows less brain activity for the option favoured by the frame (Gonzalez et al., 2005), suggesting framing also minimises effort. Practical advice: reframe important decisions both ways (Type 2 processing).

  • Getting the 72/28 and 22/78 split mixed up.
  • Not explaining why (reference point, loss aversion).
  • Forgetting the background-context factor.

Learning objectives D–E · Decision making
🎯 Learning objective · D5
❓ The question this screen answers
D5
What are common decision making strategies?

🧭 In plain words: List the strategies people use to choose among options, from compensatory (weigh everything) to non-compensatory shortcuts.

  • Compensatory: weigh all attributes (expected utility)
  • Satisficing: first good-enough option
  • Elimination by aspects: cut-offs, one attribute at a time
  • Take-the-best, recognition, default heuristics
  • Debiasing: reframe, crystal ball, break tasks down
🪝 Memory hook: Gum at the station: satisfice. A diagnosis: weigh everything.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Strategies trade accuracy for effort; good decision makers pick the strategy that fits the stakes.
Tap to open ▸
  • Expected utility / weighing all attributes (compensatory): consider every option and attribute, weight by importance and probability, and pick the best. Rational but effortful; often used only for the last few options (Payne, 1976).
  • Satisficing (Simon, 1957): consider options one by one and choose the first that meets a minimum level of acceptability. Used more when working memory is limited (Chen & Sun, 2003) and in information-heavy settings such as e-markets (Chamodrakas et al., 2010). Fine for buying gum, poor for diagnosing disease.
  • Elimination by aspects (Tversky, 1972): pick one attribute (e.g., tuition), set a cut-off (< $20,000), drop options that fail, then move to the next attribute (on the West Coast), until one option remains.
  • Take-the-best (Gigerenzer & Goldstein, 1996): decide on the single most important cue (e.g., fuel economy). A fast-and-frugal heuristic that often matches or beats complex strategies.
  • Recognition heuristic and default heuristic: choose what you recognise; stay with the option you get when you do nothing (organ donation).
  • Reframing and debiasing strategies: describe the decision as gain and as loss, use the crystal-ball technique (imagine your favoured hypothesis is wrong and explain why) against overconfidence, split projects into parts against the planning fallacy, guided reflection and listing alternatives in diagnosis (Lambe et al., 2016).
  • Mixing up satisficing and elimination by aspects.
  • No example per strategy.
  • Forgetting that strategies are often combined.

Jigsaw · The ten topics
🧩 Jigsaw topic · G1
❓ Jigsaw topic
G1
Affect heuristic

🧭 In plain words: Using your emotional reactions to make quick judgments or decisions.

  • Feeling → judgment
  • Dread → ‘more common’
  • Pachur et al. (2012); Scherer et al. (2018)
  • Fast but can mislead
🪝 Memory hook: Sharks feel deadlier than cows; cows kill more people.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Affect replaces ‘how often?’ with ‘how do I feel about it?’
Tap to open ▸

Definition. Using one’s emotional responses to influence rapid judgments or decisions (Eysenck & Keane). For risks: ‘gauge your feeling of dread that Risk A and Risk B evoke and infer that the risk with more dread is more prevalent’ (Pachur et al., 2012).

Evidence. Dread predicted people’s judged frequencies of causes of death, though availability from direct experience predicted them best (Pachur et al., 2012). People told a medical test might cause harm felt more negative affect and judged its benefits lower (Scherer et al., 2018). Sad mood increased the judged risk of formaldehyde (Lench & Darbor, 2014).

Why it matters. Feelings are fast and often useful, but feelings are not frequencies.

  • Confusing it with availability.
Jigsaw · The ten topics
🧩 Jigsaw topic · G2
❓ Jigsaw topic
G2
Base-rate neglect

🧭 In plain words: Ignoring how common something is when judging a specific case.

  • Ignore the base rate, follow the evidence
  • Taxi: 41% not 80%
  • Lawyer–engineer: .90 regardless
  • Fixed by frequencies & causal stories
🪝 Memory hook: A rare disease with a good test is still rare.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Always ask: how common is it to begin with?
Tap to open ▸

Definition. Ignoring or underweighting base-rate information (the relative frequency of an event in a population) when judging probability, usually because the specific evidence feels representative.

Evidence. Taxi-cab problem: most say 80% Blue; the Bayesian answer is 41% (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972). Lawyer–engineer: Jack judged .90 an engineer regardless of a 70:30 or 30:70 base rate (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973).

When reduced. Natural frequencies (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995), clear causal structure (faded-paint version: neglect 43% → 8%; benign-cyst mammogram; Krynski & Tenenbaum, 2007), motivation (Ditto et al., 1998), extreme base rates (.84 vs .53; Bialek, 2017).

  • Forgetting the Bayesian answer.
Jigsaw · The ten topics
🧩 Jigsaw topic · G3
❓ Jigsaw topic
G3
Bounded rationality

🧭 In plain words: We are rational, but within limits.

  • Simon (1957)
  • Rational within limits
  • Leads to satisficing, EBA
  • Gigerenzer: ecological rationality
🪝 Memory hook: Shopping with 10 minutes and €20: you can’t compare every product.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Not irrational: rational on a budget.
Tap to open ▸

Definition. Herbert Simon (1957): people are not irrational, but their rationality is bounded by limited time, information and cognitive resources. So instead of optimising, we try to get as close as possible to optimising without actually doing it.

Consequences. Heuristic strategies such as satisficing and elimination by aspects. Gigerenzer extends the idea: heuristics are the joint product of a bounded mind and the structure of the environment (ecological rationality, adaptive toolbox).

Contrast. Classical decision theory assumed unlimited rationality.

  • Equating bounded with irrational.
Jigsaw · The ten topics
🧩 Jigsaw topic · G4
❓ Jigsaw topic
G4
Elimination-by-aspects

🧭 In plain words: Removing options one attribute at a time.

  • Tversky (1972)
  • Aspect → cut-off → eliminate → repeat
  • Non-compensatory
  • Used to narrow, then compare
🪝 Memory hook: Dating-app filters: age, distance, non-smoker… one swipe at a time.
★ KEY INSIGHT · It eliminates; it never compensates.
Tap to open ▸

Definition. A choice strategy (Tversky, 1972) for when there are too many options: focus on one aspect, set a minimum criterion, eliminate options that fail it, then move to the next aspect until one option remains.

Example. Choosing a college: tuition under $20,000 (Stanford out), then on the West Coast, then… Choosing a car by total price, ignoring maintenance or insurance.

Evaluation. Fast and reduces load, but a great option can be eliminated on one minor aspect; often used to narrow down before a more careful comparison (Payne, 1976).

  • Confusing it with satisficing (which accepts the first good option).
Jigsaw · The ten topics
🧩 Jigsaw topic · G5
❓ Jigsaw topic
G5
Gambler’s fallacy

🧭 In plain words: Believing a random outcome is ‘due’.

  • ‘It’s due’
  • Ignores independence
  • Representativeness
  • Opposite of hot hand
🪝 Memory hook: Roulette: red five times, everyone bets black.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Chance has no memory.
Tap to open ▸

Definition. The mistaken belief that the probability of a random event is influenced by previous random events: after five losses, a win feels ‘due’ (Sternberg et al.).

Why. Representativeness gone awry: we expect even a short sequence to look like the long-run process (half wins), so the pattern ‘should’ change.

Correct view. Each bet or coin toss is independent; the chance is the same on the 6th as on the 1st or the 1001st.

  • Mixing it up with the hot hand.
Jigsaw · The ten topics
🧩 Jigsaw topic · G6
❓ Jigsaw topic
G6
Hot hand effect

🧭 In plain words: Believing a streak will continue.

  • ‘On fire’ belief
  • No support in shooting data
  • Opposite of gambler’s fallacy
  • Runs occur by chance
🪝 Memory hook: Three goals in a row doesn’t make the fourth more likely.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Streaks are normal in random data.
Tap to open ▸

Definition. The belief that a run of successes will continue: players and fans think a shot is more likely to go in after a hit than after a miss (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985).

Evidence. The actual shooting records show no such tendency. Opponents still guard the ‘streak shooter’ more closely.

Link. Like the gambler’s fallacy, a misperception of randomness: people underestimate how many runs occur by chance, so a run looks like a cause.

  • Saying it is the same as the gambler’s fallacy.
Jigsaw · The ten topics
🧩 Jigsaw topic · G7
❓ Jigsaw topic
G7
Illusory correlation

🧭 In plain words: Seeing a relationship that isn’t there.

  • No real relationship
  • Focus on one cell
  • Availability + confirmation
  • Stereotypes; projective tests
🪝 Memory hook: ‘It always rains when I wash my car.’
★ KEY INSIGHT · You need all four cells to see a correlation.
Tap to open ▸

Definition. Believing two variables are related when there is no (or only a weak) statistical relationship (Matlin; Hamilton & Lickel, 2000).

Mechanism. Availability: we notice and remember the one vivid cell of the 2 × 2 table (‘group X with problem Y’) and ignore the other three. In Matlin’s example 6/60 gay and 8/80 straight people have problems: both 10%, no relation.

Evidence. Chapman & Chapman (1967, 1969): clinicians saw links between Rorschach/Draw-a-Person responses (big eyes) and diagnoses (paranoia) that did not exist. Basis of many stereotypes.

  • Not mentioning the 2 × 2 table.
Jigsaw · The ten topics
🧩 Jigsaw topic · G8
❓ Jigsaw topic
G8
Recognition heuristic

🧭 In plain words: If you recognise one option, infer it is bigger/better.

  • Recognise one → choose it
  • Milan vs Modena
  • Fast and frugal; often accurate
  • Fails if recognition ≠ criterion
🪝 Memory hook: Never heard of the brand? It’s probably the smaller company.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Ignorance can be useful: knowing only one name is informative.
Tap to open ▸

Definition. When comparing two options, if you recognise one and not the other, infer that the recognised one has the higher value (Goldstein & Gigerenzer, 2002). A special case of availability.

Example. Which city is larger, Milan or Modena? Most U.S. students know only Milan, and correctly choose it (Volz et al., 2006).

Why it works. Recognition is often correlated with the criterion (big cities are mentioned more). It fails when recognition is driven by something else (Oppenheimer, 2004: famous names judged more common, unless people deliberately override it).

  • Calling it a bias only.
Jigsaw · The ten topics
🧩 Jigsaw topic · G9
❓ Jigsaw topic
G9
Satisficing

🧭 In plain words: Choosing the first option that is good enough.

  • Simon (1957)
  • First good-enough option
  • Saves time/memory
  • Depends on stakes
🪝 Memory hook: The first parking spot near enough the door.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Satisfice = satisfy + suffice.
Tap to open ▸

Definition. Considering options one by one and selecting the first that meets a minimum level of acceptability (Simon, 1957). One of the first heuristics formulated under bounded rationality.

When used. More with limited working memory (Chen & Sun, 2003); in industry where too much information impairs decisions (supplier selection in e-markets; Chamodrakas et al., 2010).

Evaluation. Sensible when in a hurry (buying gum before a train), poor for high-stakes decisions (diagnosing a disease).

  • Confusing it with optimising.
Jigsaw · The ten topics
🧩 Jigsaw topic · G10
❓ Jigsaw topic
G10
Sunk-cost effect

🧭 In plain words: Continuing because of what you already invested.

  • Past investment drives choice
  • Arkes & Blumer (1985) ski trips
  • Throwing good money after bad
  • Only future consequences matter
🪝 Memory hook: Finishing a bad film because you paid for the cinema ticket.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Sunk costs are sunk: they belong to both options.
Tap to open ▸

Definition. Continuing to invest in something because you have already invested in it and hope to recover the investment (Sternberg et al.; Arkes & Blumer, 1985).

Evidence. Ski trips: $100 Michigan vs $50 Wisconsin, same weekend, Wisconsin more enjoyable, yet most chose Michigan because ‘not going would waste more money’, though $150 is spent either way. Lemon car repairs; a miserable holiday you don’t cut short.

Why irrational. Only future costs and benefits should matter; past costs are ‘sunk’. Related to psychological accounting.

  • Forgetting that the cost is equal across options.
Resources A, B & C · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · ABC1

Explain the overestimate with the availability heuristic and the Ross and Sicoly (1979) study.

❓ Canvas question ABC1, word for word
ABC1Two spouses each estimate which proportion of the household chores they do. The sum exceeds 100%. Why?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptompeople estimate how often/how much
Diagnosisa frequency judgment = availability heuristic
Treatmentask which examples come to mind more easily, and why.
  • Availability heuristic
  • Ross & Sicoly (1979): 16 of 20 chores each
  • Own actions more available (present, encoded richly)
  • Partner’s actions often unseen
  • Also teams & lab tasks
🪝 Memory hook: You remember every time you took out the bins; you never saw your partner do it.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The total exceeds 100% because each person is judging their memory, not the household.
Tap to open ▸

This is the availability heuristic: we estimate frequency by how easily examples come to mind. Ross and Sicoly (1979) asked married partners separately which partner did more of each of 20 chores; each partner said they did more of about 16 of the 20. If both were right, each would have to do 80% of the work: 80% + 80% ≠ 100%.

Why are one’s own contributions more available? You were present and actively involved when you did a chore, so it was encoded more richly; you are often not there when your partner does theirs; and you think more about your own effort. When you then search memory for ‘who does the dishes?’, your own instances are retrieved more easily, so you judge them more frequent. Self-serving motives (seeing yourself as fair and helpful) can add to this, but Sternberg et al. stress that availability also produces errors when no self-belief is at stake (the -ing vs -n- words).

The same pattern was found in college basketball teams and in joint laboratory tasks.

  • Only saying ‘people are selfish’.
  • Not naming availability.
  • No study.
Resources A, B & C · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · ABC2

Show both orders are equally likely and explain the preference with the representativeness heuristic.

❓ Canvas question ABC2, word for word
ABC2People judge ♀♂♀♂♂♀ a more likely birth order in a family of six than ♂♀♂♂♂♂. Why?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptomone specific sequence ‘looks’ more likely
Diagnosisjudgment by similarity = representativeness
Treatmentcompute the real probability and show both are equal; explain the two ‘representative’ features.
  • Both sequences: (1/2)^6 = 1/64
  • Kahneman & Tversky (1972): 72 families
  • Representative of population (3:3)
  • Looks random (no long runs)
  • Sequence ≠ class of outcomes
🪝 Memory hook: Lottery numbers 1-2-3-4-5-6 are exactly as likely as any ‘random-looking’ set.
★ KEY INSIGHT · ‘Looks random’ is not the same as ‘is more probable’.
Tap to open ▸

Each birth is (theoretically) independent with a 1/2 chance of a girl or boy, so any exact sequence of six has probability (1/2)⁶ = 1/64. Both orders are equally likely. In Kahneman and Tversky’s (1972) study, people told that 72 families had G B G B B G estimated fewer than 72 for B G B B B B, although the best estimate is also 72.

People use the representativeness heuristic: they judge the probability of an outcome by (1) how similar it is to the population it comes from, and (2) how well it reflects the salient features of the process that generated it (Sternberg et al.). G B G B B G has three girls and three boys, matching the roughly 50:50 population; and it alternates irregularly, so it looks random. B G B B B B has five boys and a run of four, which looks neither representative nor random.

The error comes from confusing the class of outcomes (‘three girls and three boys’, which is indeed more likely than ‘five boys and one girl’) with one specific sequence. It also reflects the belief that small samples resemble the population (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971) and the underestimation of runs in random data (H T H H T H vs H H H H T H).

  • Not calculating 1/64.
  • Not naming both features of representativeness.
  • Confusing sequence with proportion.
Resources A, B & C · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · ABC3

Define confirmation bias, then show (a) how availability makes confirming evidence easier to retrieve, and (b) how anchoring makes the prior belief an anchor that is adjusted too little.

❓ Canvas question ABC3, word for word
ABC3Confirmation bias can be explained in terms of both the availability heuristic and the anchoring-and-adjustment heuristic. How?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘explain bias X with heuristic Y and Z’
Diagnosisa linking question
Treatmentdefine the bias, then show the mechanism of each heuristic step by step.
  • Definition: favour belief-consistent information
  • Availability: confirming cases easier to retrieve
  • Belief is the memory cue; counterexamples not sought
  • Anchoring: belief = anchor; adjustment too small
  • Anchor restricts the memory search
🪝 Memory hook: Your belief is both the search engine (availability) and the starting point you barely leave (anchoring).
★ KEY INSIGHT · Availability decides what evidence you see; anchoring decides how much it changes your mind.
Tap to open ▸

Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, favour and recall information that confirms prior beliefs.

Via availability. We judge how often something is true by how easily examples come to mind. Confirming cases are more available: we noticed them (they fitted our expectation), encoded them better, rehearsed them, and when we search memory we use our belief as the cue, so confirming instances come back first. Disconfirming cases were often not noticed or were dismissed, so they are hard to retrieve. Matlin shows this in illusory correlations: people attend to the one cell that confirms the stereotype and ignore the other three, and ‘examples that confirm our hypotheses are readily available, but we resist searching for counterexamples’ (a cause of overconfidence). Sternberg et al. add that instances that fit our biased expectations ‘are more likely to be available in memory’.

Via anchoring and adjustment. Our prior belief acts as the anchor. New evidence should move us, but adjustments from an anchor are typically insufficient. So contradicting evidence shifts the belief only slightly, and we stay close to what we believed. The anchor also restricts the memory search to information close to it (Matlin). Matlin explicitly groups confirmation bias, belief bias and illusory correlation with anchoring as examples of endorsing current hypotheses rather than questioning them (top-down processing).

  • Explaining only one heuristic.
  • Defining the heuristics without linking them to the bias.
  • No reference to illusory correlation/Matlin.
Resources A, B & C · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · ABC4

Use overconfidence and its causes, the availability heuristic and hindsight to explain why people think they would notice.

❓ Canvas question ABC4, word for word
ABC4Nearly 90% of people believe they would spot the gorilla in the inattentional-blindness video. Explain this using this problem’s literature.
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptompeople are too sure about their own ability
Diagnosisoverconfidence (plus availability)
Treatmentname the bias, its causes from the readings, and contrast belief with actual performance.
  • Overconfidence: belief > performance
  • Misses aren’t stored → availability favours noticing
  • Counterexamples not sought
  • Knowing the gorilla is there = hindsight/anchor
  • Vivid description makes it seem obvious
🪝 Memory hook: Ask people if they’d see a gorilla and they picture the gorilla, not the passes.
★ KEY INSIGHT · You can’t remember what you never noticed, so your memory tells you that you always notice.
Tap to open ▸

In the actual studies about half of viewers miss the gorilla (Problem 1), yet nearly 90% believe they would see it. This is overconfidence: confidence that is higher than performance justifies (Matlin). People overestimate their own skills and judgment in many areas (100% confident, 80% right; Fischhoff et al., 1977).

Availability. When people judge ‘would I notice something unusual?’, they search memory for examples. Instances when they did notice unexpected things are available; instances when they missed something are, by definition, not in memory, because they never noticed them. So the evidence that comes to mind is one-sided, and missing seems rare.

Reasons for overconfidence (Matlin): people are unaware their knowledge rests on tenuous assumptions (here, the intuition that attention captures anything salient), confirming examples are available while counterexamples are not sought, and alternative possibilities are not taken seriously.

Hindsight / knowing the outcome. People asked the question already know there is a gorilla; with that knowledge it seems obvious and impossible to miss, like the hindsight bias where the known outcome becomes the anchor and the adjustment is too small. The description ‘a gorilla walks through a basketball game’ is also vivid and makes the gorilla mentally salient in a way it is not while counting passes.

  • Only saying ‘people are overconfident’ without a mechanism.
  • Not linking to availability.
  • Claiming exact figures without checking Problem 1.
Resources A, B & C · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · ABC5

Show that the believer looks at one cell of a 2 × 2 table; the skeptic asks for the other three.

❓ Canvas question ABC5, word for word
ABC5People burn a candle for a positive outcome and justify it by recalling times it worked. How would a skeptic counter this using the research on heuristics?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘I remember times X went with Y’
Diagnosisillusory correlation via availability (+ confirmation bias)
Treatmentdraw the 2 × 2 table and show the missing cells.
  • Illusory correlation
  • Need all four cells
  • Hits available, misses forgotten
  • Confirmation bias: no attempt to disconfirm
  • Compare outcome rate with vs without candle
🪝 Memory hook: Lucky socks ‘work’ because you only remember the matches you won in them.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A correlation needs a comparison: what happens without the candle?
Tap to open ▸

The skeptic would point to an illusory correlation: a perceived relationship between two variables (candle burning and good outcomes) without statistical evidence. To know whether candles work you need all four cells of a 2 × 2 table: (1) candle + good outcome, (2) candle + no good outcome, (3) no candle + good outcome, (4) no candle + no good outcome. The believer only cites cell 1.

Why only cell 1? The availability heuristic: hits are memorable and get retold, so they come to mind easily; misses are forgotten or explained away (‘I didn’t pray hard enough’), and outcomes that happened without a candle are never connected to candles at all. This is also confirmation bias: we look for evidence that confirms the belief and do not try to disconfirm it (Matlin). Hindsight can add to it: after a good outcome, it feels as if it was always going to happen once the candle was lit.

The skeptic’s counter: ‘Tell me how often you lit a candle and nothing happened, and how often good things happened without a candle. If good outcomes are just as common without the candle, there is no relationship.’ Like Matlin’s welfare example, the number of hits is meaningless without the other cells.

  • Only saying ‘coincidence’.
  • Not drawing/naming the 2 × 2 table.
  • Missing availability as the mechanism.
Resources A, B & C · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · ABC6

Define both, show the probability rule each violates, give the classic example of each, and the explanation.

❓ Canvas question ABC6, word for word
ABC6What is the difference between the conjunction fallacy and the double conjunction fallacy?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘A and B’ vs ‘A’
Diagnosisconjunction rule
Treatmentwrite P(A&B) ≤ P(A) and P(A&B) ≤ P(B), then check how many are violated.
  • Rule: P(A&B) ≤ P(A), P(B)
  • Single: conjunction > one constituent (Linda)
  • Double: conjunction > both constituents
  • Crupi et al. (2018): 49% of medical experts
  • Representativeness vs hypothesis-support account
🪝 Memory hook: ‘Rain and wind’ can’t be likelier than ‘rain’, nor likelier than ‘wind’.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Single breaks the rule once; double breaks it twice.
Tap to open ▸

The conjunction rule: the probability of two events together can never exceed the probability of either one alone: P(A & B) ≤ P(A) and P(A & B) ≤ P(B).

The conjunction fallacy is judging the conjunction more probable than one of its constituents: Linda is judged more likely to be a ‘feminist bank teller’ than a ‘bank teller’ (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983), although all feminist bank tellers are bank tellers. Other examples: men over 55 and had a heart attack (30%) vs had a heart attack (18%); seven-letter words ending in -ing vs with n in sixth place.

The double conjunction fallacy is a stronger form: the conjunction is judged more probable than each of its constituents separately: P(A & B) > P(A) and P(A & B) > P(B). Crupi et al. (2018) found 49% of medical experts judged a man with chronic anaemia more likely to have alcoholism and thalassemia trait than to have alcoholism, or to have thalassemia trait.

Explanation: the standard account is representativeness (the added detail makes the description more typical). Tentori et al. (2013) argue it is the hypothesis that is strongly supported by the evidence (Linda + black shoes test); the double conjunction findings fit this, because the clinical evidence strongly supported the combined diagnosis.

  • Defining the double fallacy as two fallacies in a row.
  • No probability notation or rule.
  • No study for the double fallacy.
Resources A, B & C · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · ABC7

Calculate the expected hit rate of matching vs always predicting red, and explain why people match.

❓ Canvas question ABC7, word for word
ABC7In Tversky and Edwards’ experiment, red lit on 70% of trials and green on 30%. Participants said ‘red’ on 70% and ‘green’ on 30% of trials. Why is this suboptimal, and how is it representativeness?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘which strategy gives the most hits?’
Diagnosiscompare expected accuracy of two strategies (probability matching vs maximising)
Treatmentcompute P(hit) for each.
  • Matching: .7² + .3² = .58
  • Maximising: .70
  • Each green guess right only 30% of the time
  • People want predictions to look like outcomes
  • Representativeness + gambler’s-fallacy thinking
🪝 Memory hook: A weather app that says ‘rain’ on random 70% of days is right less often than one that always says ‘rain’ in a 70%-rain town.
★ KEY INSIGHT · When outcomes are random, copying the pattern is worse than betting on the favourite every time.
Tap to open ▸

Probability matching (red 70%, green 30%), with predictions independent of the random lights: P(hit) = P(say red) × P(red) + P(say green) × P(green) = .70 × .70 + .30 × .30 = .49 + .09 = .58.

Maximising (always say red): P(hit) = 1 × .70 = .70. Always predicting the more frequent outcome gives 12 more hits per 100 trials. Any green guess has only a .30 chance of being right, worse than a red guess at .70, so every switch to green lowers the expected score.

Why do people match? The representativeness heuristic: people want their sequence of predictions to resemble the sequence of outcomes, a mix of about 70% red and 30% green that looks random and representative of the process. Always saying red looks unrepresentative (‘green will surely come up’), similar to the gambler’s fallacy (after several reds, green feels ‘due’). But the individual outcomes are independent and unpredictable, so the best strategy is to ignore patterns and always choose the most likely option.

  • Not doing the calculation.
  • Saying people are ‘right’ because the proportions match.
  • Not linking to representativeness.
Resources A, B & C · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · ABC8

Explain the ‘man-who’ argument (Nisbett & Ross, 1980) as believing a tiny sample represents the population.

❓ Canvas question ABC8, word for word
ABC8Explain how ‘man-who’ arguments (‘I know a man who smoked his whole life and lived to 106’) are the representativeness heuristic gone wrong.
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptomone vivid case vs statistics
Diagnosissmall-sample representativeness (‘man-who’)
Treatmentname sample size and base rates as the ignored information.
  • Anecdote vs statistics (Nisbett & Ross, 1980)
  • Small sample assumed to represent population
  • Ignores sample size and base rates
  • Vivid = available
  • Exceptions don’t refute probabilities
🪝 Memory hook: ‘My grandma never wore a seatbelt’ doesn’t make seatbelts useless.
★ KEY INSIGHT · An anecdote is a sample of one; statistics are a sample of thousands.
Tap to open ▸

A ‘man-who’ argument refutes statistics with a personal anecdote: ‘I know a man who…’ (Nisbett & Ross, 1980; Sternberg et al.).

It is representativeness gone wrong because people mistakenly believe that small samples resemble the population from which they are drawn (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971). A sample of one is treated as if it represents everyone who smokes. People ignore sample size (one case vs thousands in the statistics) and base rates (most smokers have shorter lives; the statistic is about probabilities, not certainties). Matlin notes representativeness is so appealing that we ignore sample size and base rate.

The anecdote is also vivid and available, which makes it feel important. But a probabilistic claim (‘smoking raises the risk of early death’) is not refuted by an exception: some smokers will live long by chance, just as some non-smokers die young.

  • Calling it availability only.
  • Not mentioning sample size.
  • Not explaining probability vs certainty.
Resources A, B & C · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · ABC9

Compute P(disease | positive) step by step, then explain why intuition says ‘about 95%’.

❓ Canvas question ABC9, word for word
ABC9A rare disease affects 1%. Test sensitivity 95%, specificity 90%. What is the probability that a patient who tests positive has the disease? Does it match your intuition?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptombase rate + hit rate + false-alarm rate, asking P(disease | positive)
DiagnosisBayes / base-rate problem
Treatmentturn percentages into natural frequencies (e.g., 10,000 people), fill a tree, divide true positives by all positives.
  • Use 10,000 people
  • 95 true +, 990 false +
  • 95 / 1,085 ≈ 9%
  • Intuition ~95% = base-rate neglect
  • Frequencies make it intuitive
🪝 Memory hook: Looking for 1 needle among 99 straws: even a good magnet picks up lots of straw.
★ KEY INSIGHT · With a rare disease, most positives are false positives, even with a good test.
Tap to open ▸

Step 1: imagine 10,000 people (natural frequencies; Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995).

  • Base rate 1% → 100 have the disease; 9,900 do not.
  • Sensitivity 95% → of the 100 sick, 95 test positive (true positives).
  • Specificity 90% → of the 9,900 healthy, 90% test negative, so 10% = 990 test positive (false positives).

Step 2: all positives = 95 + 990 = 1,085.

Step 3: P(disease | positive) = 95 / 1,085 ≈ .088, about 9%. With Bayes’ theorem: (.01 × .95) / [(.01 × .95) + (.99 × .10)] = .0095 / .1085 ≈ .088.

Intuition. Most people guess around 90–95%. This is base-rate neglect: we focus on the test’s accuracy (the evidence, which is representative of disease) and ignore that the disease is rare, so the many healthy people generate far more false positives (990) than the few sick people generate true positives (95). The same happens in the mammogram problem (Krynski & Tenenbaum, 2007). Natural frequencies make the answer much easier to see (16% vs 46% correct; Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995).

Test +Test −Total
Disease955100
No disease9908,9109,900
Total1,0858,91510,000
  • Answering 95% (sensitivity).
  • Using 90% instead of 10% as false-positive rate.
  • Not explaining the intuition.
Resources A, B & C · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · ABC10

Use hindsight bias (and its anchoring explanation), confirmation bias, overconfidence and illusory correlation to explain why HARKing feels legitimate to researchers.

❓ Canvas question ABC10, word for word
ABC10How can you explain HARKing (Hypothesizing After Results are Known) using this problem’s literature?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptomafter knowing an outcome, people think they predicted it
Diagnosishindsight bias (+ confirmation, overconfidence, illusory correlation)
Treatmentdefine the bias, give its mechanism, and map it onto the researcher’s behaviour.
  • Hindsight bias: ‘knew it all along’
  • Known result = 100% anchor; adjustment too small
  • Memory reconstructed (Carli, 1999)
  • Confirmation bias, illusory correlation
  • Overconfidence in own theory; hinders learning
🪝 Memory hook: Shooting the arrow first and painting the target around it afterwards.
★ KEY INSIGHT · HARKing is hindsight bias with a publication deadline.
Tap to open ▸

Hindsight bias: once we know an outcome, we believe it was predictable and that we ‘knew it all along’ (Matlin; Sternberg et al.). People cannot predict experimental results above chance in advance, but after hearing them they say they were obvious. After obtaining their results, researchers find the new hypothesis ‘obvious’ and may sincerely feel they could have predicted it, so presenting it as the original hypothesis does not feel dishonest.

Mechanism (anchoring). The known result acts as an anchor of 100% certainty, and people do not adjust their sense of predictability downward enough (Matlin). In addition, memory is reconstructed to fit the outcome (Carli, 1999): researchers may misremember what they originally expected.

Confirmation and my-side bias. Researchers search their data and the literature for information consistent with the result and select the hypothesis that fits, rather than trying to disconfirm it. Illusory correlation: a chance pattern in the data is seen as a real relationship and then explained. Overconfidence in one’s own theory adds to it (scientists are overconfident about their theories; Trout, 2002).

Sternberg et al. note that hindsight bias ‘hinders learning’: if the outcome always seems expected, there is nothing to learn. In science that is costly: HARKing turns chance findings into apparently confirmed predictions.

  • Only calling it ‘dishonest’ without a cognitive explanation.
  • Not naming hindsight bias.
  • No mechanism (anchoring/reconstruction).
Resources D & E · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · DE1

Define both concepts, show how they relate, and how each is evaluated.

❓ Canvas question DE1, word for word
DE1This problem is about judgment and decision making. What is the difference between the two?
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘what is the difference between X and Y’
Diagnosisdefinition + contrast
Treatmentdefine both, give an example, show how they connect.
  • Judgment = likelihood estimate; accuracy
  • Decision = choosing among options; involves risk
  • Judgment is input for decisions
  • Party example (Robinson-Riegler)
  • Good decision ≠ good outcome
🪝 Memory hook: Weather forecast = judgment; taking an umbrella = decision.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Judgment asks ‘how likely?’; decision asks ‘what will I do?’
Tap to open ▸

Judgment is assessing the likelihood of events on the basis of incomplete information (e.g., judging the chance you will pass the next exam). What matters is accuracy. Decision making is selecting one option from several possibilities (which university to attend; Coke or Pepsi); if full information is unavailable, judgment is required (Eysenck & Keane). It differs from problem solving, where you must generate the solutions yourself.

Relation. Judgment is typically an important initial part of decision making: someone buying a car judges running costs, reliability and enjoyment, then chooses. Robinson-Riegler’s example: ‘What are the chances Tom will be at the party?’ is a judgment; ‘let’s go’ is the decision. Decision making adds a choice between alternatives and therefore risk: the choice can be wrong.

Evaluation. Judgments are evaluated by accuracy against reality; decisions are often (unfairly) evaluated by their consequences, but a decision can be good given the information at the time even if the outcome is poor (‘the operation was a success, unfortunately the patient died’).

  • Giving only one definition.
  • No link between the two.
  • Evaluating decisions only by outcome.
Resources D & E · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · DE2

Explain what a ‘prospect’ is and why a theory of choices between prospects is named this way.

❓ Canvas question DE2, word for word
DE2Explain the name ‘prospect theory’.
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘why is it called…’
Diagnosisunpack the key term
Treatmentsay what a ‘prospect’ is and what the theory does with it.
  • Prospect = risky option (outcomes + probabilities)
  • Theory of how people evaluate prospects
  • Kahneman & Tversky (1979)
  • Changes from a reference point, not final states
  • Descriptive, not normative
🪝 Memory hook: ‘What are my prospects?’ = what could happen to me from here.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Prospect theory = a theory of how people look at what they might gain or lose.
Tap to open ▸

In decision research a prospect is a risky option: a gamble with possible outcomes and their probabilities (e.g., ‘1/3 chance that 600 people will be saved, 2/3 chance that nobody will be saved’, or ‘80% chance to win $4’). Kahneman and Tversky (1979) developed a theory of how people evaluate such prospects and choose between them under risk, hence ‘prospect theory’. (The name is not explained in your readings; this is the standard meaning of the term in their 1979 paper, Prospect theory: An analysis of decision under risk.)

The word also fits the theory’s core idea: people evaluate the prospect of a change, what they stand to gain or lose from where they are now (the reference point), rather than final states of wealth, as expected utility theory assumes (Robinson-Riegler). It is a descriptive theory: it aims to describe how people actually value prospects and why their choices violate expected utility.

  • Saying it is about ‘the future’ only.
  • Not mentioning risk/gambles.
  • Calling it normative.
Resources D & E · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · DE3

Describe the value function: reference point, gains vs losses, concave vs convex, and loss aversion (steeper for losses).

❓ Canvas question DE3, word for word
DE3Prospect theory proposes a function that expresses subjective value as a function of actual value. Explain its main characteristics.
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptoma graph of subjective vs actual value
Diagnosisthe value function
Treatmentdescribe origin, shape right, shape left, steepness.
  • Origin = reference point (current state)
  • Gains: concave (diminishing)
  • Losses: convex
  • Steeper for losses = loss aversion
  • Reference point can shift → framing
🪝 Memory hook: Losing €50 hurts more than finding €50 makes you happy.
★ KEY INSIGHT · An S-shaped curve, kinked at the reference point, steeper on the loss side.
Tap to open ▸

1. Reference point. The origin of the graph is the current state (‘what we have right now’). Outcomes are coded as gains (right) or losses (left) relative to it, not as absolute amounts.

2. Concave for gains. Subjective value rises with gains, but increasingly slowly (diminishing sensitivity): going from €0 to €100 feels bigger than from €1,000 to €1,100.

3. Convex for losses. Negative value also grows less and less steeply as losses get bigger.

4. Steeper for losses: loss aversion. The curve is steeper on the loss side: ‘we feel losses more acutely than we feel gains; the psychological pain associated with losing $50 is greater than the psychological pleasure of gaining $50’ (Robinson-Riegler, Figure 11.4).

5. Consequence. Because the reference point can shift, the same outcome can be valued differently depending on how it is presented, so preferences change when the reference point changes (framing).

  • Drawing it symmetric.
  • Forgetting the reference point.
  • Mixing up concave and convex.
Resources D & E · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · DE4

Use the curvature (concave gains, convex losses) to compare a sure option with a gamble of equal expected value.

❓ Canvas question DE4, word for word
DE4Explain how this function shows why people are risk averse for gains and risk prone for losses.
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘use the curve to explain risk attitudes’
Diagnosiscompare v(sure) with p × v(gamble) on a concave vs convex curve
Treatmentpick one equal-expected-value example for each side and read values off the curve.
  • Same expected value, different subjective value
  • Concave gains: v(sure) > p × v(big) → risk averse
  • Convex losses: sure loss feels worse → risk seeking
  • Loss aversion adds to it
  • Stress amplifies both (Porcelli & Delgado, 2009)
🪝 Memory hook: Bird in the hand when winning; double-or-nothing when losing.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The bend of the curve is the risk attitude: concave = play safe; convex = gamble.
Tap to open ▸

Take the Asian disease problem. Both options have the same expected value (200 saved = 1/3 × 600 saved).

Gains (concave). Because the curve flattens, v(600) is less than 3 × v(200): saving 600 does not feel three times as good as saving 200. So the sure gain, v(200), is worth more than the gamble, 1/3 × v(600). People choose the sure thing: risk averse (72% chose Program A).

Losses (convex). On the loss side the curve also flattens: 600 deaths do not feel three times as bad as 200, and −v(600) × 2/3 is less negative than −v(400). The sure loss of 400 feels worse than a 2/3 chance of losing 600 (with a 1/3 chance of losing nothing). People gamble: risk prone (78% chose Program D).

Loss aversion strengthens the effect: losses are felt more acutely, so people are especially motivated to avoid a sure loss. Porcelli and Delgado (2009) showed that acute stress makes both tendencies stronger (risky choices: .42 gains vs .61 losses without stress; .33 vs .66 under stress).

  • Only stating the result (72%/78%) without using the curve.
  • Mixing up which side is concave.
  • Not showing expected values are equal.
Resources D & E · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · DE5

Show that demo 12.7 (lost ticket vs lost €20) manipulates background context, and demo 12.8 (lives saved vs lives lost) manipulates wording.

❓ Canvas question DE5, word for word
DE5Use (i) background context and (ii) wording/framing to explain the difference between demonstrations 12.7 and 12.8 in Matlin.
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptomtwo demos with identical maths, different choices
Diagnosisframing; identify which factor changes in each
Treatmentfor each demo: what is identical, what differs, results, explanation.
  • 12.7 = background context; 12.8 = wording
  • 12.7: 46% vs 88% (mental accounts)
  • 12.8: 72% A vs 78% D
  • Both: same maths, different choices
  • Both violate rational consistency
🪝 Memory hook: Ticket in the ‘fun’ account vs cash in the ‘wallet’ account; ‘saved’ vs ‘die’.
★ KEY INSIGHT · 12.7 changes what happened; 12.8 changes how it is said.
Tap to open ▸

Matlin: the framing effect shows that decisions are influenced by (1) the background context of the choice and (2) the way the question is worded.

Demo 12.7: background context. In both problems you lose €20 and must decide whether to pay €20 for a concert ticket; financially identical. What differs is the background: in Problem 1 the lost item is the ticket, in Problem 2 a €20 note. We keep mental accounts by topic: a lost ticket is charged to the ‘concert account’, so buying another makes the concert cost €40, which feels too much (only 46% would buy). The lost note comes from general cash and is seen as irrelevant to the concert (88% would buy; Kahneman & Tversky, 1984).

Demo 12.8: wording. The context (600 people, two programmes) and the outcomes are identical; only the wording changes from lives saved (gain frame) to lives lost (loss frame). With gain wording 72% chose the sure option A (risk averse); with loss wording 78% chose the risky option D (risk seeking; Tversky & Kahneman, 1981). The words move the reference point, so the same outcome is coded as a gain or a loss.

So: in 12.7 the situation surrounding the choice changes (what was lost); in 12.8 only the description of the outcomes changes.

Demo 12.7Demo 12.8
FactorBackground contextWording of the question
What is identicalMoney lost and ticket price (€20)Outcomes and probabilities
What differsLost ticket vs lost €20 noteLives saved vs lives lost
Result46% vs 88% buy72% sure (gain) vs 78% risky (loss)
MechanismMental accountingReference point; risk averse vs risk seeking
  • Treating both demos as wording effects.
  • Wrong percentages.
  • Not explaining mental accounting.
Resources D & E · Tutorial questions
🧠 In-depth question · DE6

Define invariance, show the two problems describe the same options, and show that preferences reverse.

❓ Canvas question DE6, word for word
DE6Explain how demonstration 12.8 is an example of a violation of invariance (an assumption of expected utility theory).
🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘violation of an assumption’
Diagnosisstate the principle, then show the data contradict it
Treatmentdefine invariance, show A≡C and B≡D, show preferences reverse.
  • Invariance: description should not matter
  • A ≡ C; B ≡ D (same expected value)
  • 72% A vs 78% D: preference reverses
  • Frame decides, not options
  • Also: preference reversals (Lichtenstein & Slovic)
🪝 Memory hook: Same pizza, cut in 8 or 4 slices: if you’d only eat the 8-slice version, invariance is broken.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Invariance says the label can’t change the choice; demo 12.8 shows it does.
Tap to open ▸

Invariance is a normative principle of expected utility theory: a decision maker’s choices should not depend on the way the choice is presented. If you prefer A to B in one description, you should prefer the same option in any equivalent description (Robinson-Riegler).

Demo 12.8. Of 600 people: Program A, ‘200 will be saved’, is the same outcome as Program C, ‘400 will die’. Program B, ‘1/3 chance 600 saved, 2/3 chance none saved’, is the same prospect as Program D, ‘1/3 chance nobody dies, 2/3 chance 600 die’. All four options have the same expected value (200 survivors).

The violation. If preferences were invariant, people who choose A should choose C, and people who choose B should choose D. Instead 72% chose A over B, but 78% chose D over C: the majority preference reverses between two descriptions of the same choice (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981). The preference depends on the frame (gains vs losses), not on the options, so invariance is violated.

This is why expected utility is a poor descriptive model, and why prospect theory (reference point, risk aversion for gains, risk seeking for losses) was proposed. Preference reversals between choosing and pricing gambles (Lichtenstein & Slovic, 1971, 1973) are another violation of invariance.

  • Not showing that A=C and B=D.
  • Defining invariance vaguely.
  • Not linking to expected utility as normative.
