Block A–B · Judgement Under Uncertainty

❓ How should we judge probabilities, how do we actually judge them, and when do our shortcuts lead us astray?

🚕A.1

Judgement, decision making and the Bayesian ideal

❓ This lecture answers: What is the difference between judging and deciding, and how should we update a belief when new evidence arrives?
A.1.1
Two overlapping skills

⚖️ Judgement = how likely something is, from incomplete information (yardstick: accuracy). Decision making = choosing one option, which adds choice and so risk. Judge a decision by the information available, not only by its outcome.

A.1.2
The rules of probability

🎲 Lee is 1 of 10 candidates: P = 0.1; not getting it = 0.9; Lee or the roommate = 0.2. Conditional probability = P(A given B), calculated with Bayes’ theorem (Sternberg).

A.1.3
Bayes’ theorem in plain words

🔄 Bayesian inference: prior probabilities + new evidence → posterior probabilities (90% sure of a lie → 60% after someone confirms the story). posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio.

A.1.4
Worked example: the taxi-cab problem

🚕 Kahneman & Tversky (1972): 85% Green cabs, 15% Blue; the witness says “Blue” and is wrong 20% of the time. 12 true vs 17 false “Blue” reports → 12/29 ≈ 41%, not 80%.

INTERACTIVE · BAYES WITH 100 DOTS

🚕 Play with the taxi-cab problem

Each dot is one accident. Change how common Blue cabs are and how accurate the witness is. Blue = Blue cab correctly called Blue; red = Green cab wrongly called Blue. The answer is blue dots ÷ all coloured dots.

Blue cabs in the city: 15%
Witness accuracy: 80%
🔔
THINK OF IT LIKE…A smoke alarm that's right 80% of the time in a house where fires are rare. Most times it goes off, it's burnt toast. A reliable signal about a rare event still produces mostly false alarms.
✗ THE MISTAKEConcluding that a decision was bad because it turned out badly.
✓ CORRECTDecision quality depends on the information available when the decision was made. A good decision can have a poor outcome (Eysenck & Keane): “The operation was a success. Unfortunately, the patient died.”
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDJudging is guessing how likely something is; deciding is picking what to do. To guess well, combine how common something is with how strong the new clue is. In the taxi problem the witness is pretty good, but Blue cabs are so rare that she’s wrong more often than right when she says “Blue”.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKPosterior = prior × evidence. Rare stays fairly rare.
✎ EXAM TIPPractise the taxi-cab sum both ways: with odds (.15 × .80 vs .85 × .20 = 12:17) and with counts (12 of 29). The counts version is easier under exam stress.
▶ Find a video: Bayes and the taxi-cab problem
✅ Quick check: What do the “prior odds” and the “likelihood ratio” each represent?

Prior odds: how likely hypothesis A is compared with B before the new data (taxi: .15 / .85). Likelihood ratio: how likely the observed data would be if A were true compared with if B were true (witness says “Blue”: .80 / .20). Multiply them to get the posterior odds (12 : 17).

✅ Quick check: If 50% of cabs were Blue, what would P(Blue) be?

80%. With equal priors (odds 1:1) the posterior is just the likelihood ratio 80:20. Try it with the slider.

👔A.2

Neglecting base rates: the representativeness heuristic

❓ This lecture answers: Why do people ignore base rates, and what is the representativeness heuristic?
A.2.1
Base-rate neglect

👔 The base rate = how common something is in the population. Lawyer-engineer problem (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973): Jack judged .90 engineer regardless of a 70:30 or 30:70 split. Doctors rely on base rates: chest pain at 10 vs at 60.

A.2.2
Heuristics: rules of thumb

🧰 Heuristics ignore part of the information to decide quickly and frugally (Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier, 2011). Matlin & Farmer: they are typically accurate; errors come from over-relying on them.

A.2.3
The representativeness heuristic

🪞 Judging by how typical something looks of a category or of the random process. G B G B B G and B G B B B B are equally likely ((1/2)⁶; 72 each). Symptoms: the law of small numbers, man-who arguments, the gambler’s fallacy and hot hand.

INTERACTIVE · DOES THE COIN REMEMBER?

🪙 Gambler's fallacy simulator

We flip a fair coin 100,000 times and look only at flips that came right after 5 tails in a row. Is heads now "due"? illustrative simulation

Related symptoms: the law of small numbers (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971) and man-who arguments, “I know a man who … lived to 110” (Nisbett & Ross, 1980). The opposite of the gambler’s fallacy is the hot hand: basketball records show no streaks (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985). Magicians and con artists exploit our poor sense of chance, for example with birthday coincidences in small groups (Krantz, 1992).

QUICK POLL

👶 Which family of six is more likely?

🪞
THINK OF IT LIKE…Judging a book by its cover. Jack "looks like" an engineer, so you forget that the pile you drew him from was 70% lawyers.
✗ THE MISTAKE"GBGBBG is more likely because three of each is more common."
✓ CORRECT"Three of each" as a type is more common, but each specific order has the same probability, (1/2)⁶.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDRepresentativeness means judging by resemblance: Jack sounds like an engineer, so he must be one, even if 70% of the people in the pile are lawyers. It also makes “random-looking” sequences seem more likely, makes one anecdote feel like proof, and makes gamblers think they’re “due”.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKLooks like it → must be it (and forget how common it is).
✎ EXAM TIPLearn the four “symptoms” of representativeness: base-rate neglect, the law of small numbers, man-who arguments, and the gambler’s fallacy / hot hand. Each one is a possible Canvas or exam question.
✅ Quick check: How are the gambler’s fallacy and the hot hand opposite errors with the same root?

The gambler’s fallacy expects a run to end (“I’m due”); the hot hand expects a run to continue. Both treat independent events as if they were linked: we expect sequences to look the way chance “should” look (representativeness), but a coin or a shot has no memory.

▶ Find a video: representativeness heuristic▶ Find a video: gambler's fallacy and hot hand
🏦A.3

The conjunction fallacy: when more detail feels more likely

❓ This lecture answers: Why do people rate "A and B" above "A", and do experts do it too?
TRY IT FIRST

🏦 Linda (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983)

"Linda is 31, single, outspoken and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student she was deeply concerned with discrimination and social justice, and took part in anti-nuclear demonstrations."

Which is more likely?

Replicated many times (Fisk, 2004; Kahneman & Frederick, 2005).

A.3.1
Linda the bank teller

🏦 “Teller and feminist” rated above “teller”: the conjunction fallacy (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983), from representativeness (Swoyer, 2002). It persists with clear wording (Sides et al., 2002), and students with high SAT scores show it more (Stanovich, 2011).

A.3.2
A different explanation: support, not probability

👟 Tentori et al. (2013): the description strongly supports “feminist”. “Teller and owns black shoes” is more probable but unsupported, and the results favoured the hypothesis-support explanation.

A.3.3
Experts are not immune

🩺 Croskerry missed McKinley’s heart attack: he looked representative of healthy people. Double conjunction fallacy: 49% of medical experts (Crupi et al., 2018). Medical experts can fall for both kinds. Common medical biases: anchoring, omission bias, overconfidence (Saposnik et al., 2016).

PREDICT · TENTORI ET AL. (2013)

👟 Probability or support?

A new option: “Linda is a bank teller and owns a pair of black shoes.” Owning black shoes is more probable than being a feminist activist, but Linda’s description gives it no support at all. What does each account predict?

Probability account
“teller + black shoes” should be rated likelier than “teller + feminist”.
Support account
“teller + feminist” should be rated likelier, because the description is good evidence for it.
🕵️
THINK OF IT LIKE…A detective story: "the butler did it with a knife in the library" sounds more convincing than "the butler did it", yet every extra detail is one more thing that has to be true.
✗ THE MISTAKE"The error is believing Linda is a feminist."
✓ CORRECTThat belief is reasonable. The error is ranking "teller and feminist" above "teller".
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDAdding detail to a story makes it feel more likely but actually makes it less likely: “bank teller who’s a feminist” can never beat plain “bank teller”. People still pick it, even smart students and doctors, because the detail fits the description so well.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKMore detail, more believable, less probable.
✎ EXAM TIPRemember the frequency rescue: 65% fell for the heart-attack conjunction with percentages but only 25% with “how many of 1,000 men” (Sternberg). It links A.3 to A.5.
✅ Quick check: Can the conjunction fallacy also come from availability?

Yes. People estimate more seven-letter words ending in “-ing” than words with “n” in the sixth position, although the second set contains the first (Tversky & Kahneman, 1983). The “-ing” words are easier to bring to mind, so the conjunction fallacy can arise from either heuristic.

✅ Quick check: Single vs double conjunction fallacy?

Single: “A and B” rated above one part (Linda). Double: “A and B” rated above each part separately, as 49% of medical experts did with alcoholism and thalassemia trait (Crupi et al., 2018). The double version is the stronger violation.

▶ Find a video: the Linda problem
💭A.4

The availability heuristic

❓ This lecture answers: How does ease of recall drive our frequency judgements, what distorts it, and how does it create illusory correlations?
TRY IT · 20 SECONDS

🔤 R first, or R third?

Type as many words as you can that start with R, then as many with R as the third letter (10 seconds each).

Ready?
A.4.1
Ease of recall as a clue to frequency

💭 Availability: frequency judged by how easily examples come to mind (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973): Illinois vs Idaho students. Usually accurate. Representativeness asks if an example is similar to a category; availability asks you to recall examples.

A.4.2
Classic demonstrations

🔤 More words have R third than begin with R. Each spouse claimed 16 of the 20 chores (Ross & Sicoly, 1979). Much-publicised causes of death, such as murder, are judged likelier (Lichtenstein et al., 1978).

A.4.3
Which availability? Experience, media or dread

😨 Pachur et al. (2012a): direct experience predicted judged causes of death best, the affect heuristic (dread) also did, media worst. Availability can be overridden, but not under cognitive load: famous name chosen 80% (Oppenheimer & Monin, 2009).

A.4.4
What contaminates availability: recency and familiarity

📰 Recency (MacLeod & Campbell, 1992) and familiarity: El Salvador ≈ Indonesia, though Indonesia is 35× larger (Brown & Siegler, 1992). Dr Alter’s “pneumonia” was aspirin toxicity (Groopman, 2007). Fix: Type 2 thinking, guided reflection, alternative diagnoses.

A.4.5
The recognition heuristic: availability done right

🏙️ Recognise Milan but not Modena? Pick Milan: the recognition heuristic gives the right answer (Goldstein & Gigerenzer, 2002). A special case of availability that often works.

A.4.6
Illusory correlation

🔗 Seeing a link without real evidence, a source of stereotypes (Reber, 2004; Risen et al., 2007). Use all four cells of a 2 × 2 table: 6 of 60 vs 8 of 80 is 10% each, so no link.

QUIZ · TELL THE HEURISTICS APART

🧭 Similar, recall or start point?

🪞 RepresentativenessYou are given an example: is it similar to a category? (Linda, Jack)
💭 AvailabilityYou are given a category: how easily can you recall examples? (R-words, chores)
⚓ AnchoringWhere did I start, and did I adjust enough? (8 × 7 × 6 … × 1)

Which heuristic? Tap a case.

PREDICT · OPPENHEIMER (2004)

🧠 Can availability be switched off?

Which of two surnames is more common, a famous one or a non-famous one? Availability should favour the famous name.

Affect also colours judgements: a test described as possibly harmful was judged less beneficial (Scherer et al., 2018), and repeated false statements (“a date is a dried plum”) felt truer even to people who knew the answer (Fazio et al., 2015).

INTERACTIVE · ILLUSORY CORRELATION

🕯️ Does burning a candle help?

Fill in all four cells (imagine 40 hopes). A link exists only if a good outcome is more frequent with a candle than without. Most people look only at cell 1. illustrative (Canvas Question 5)

Matlin & Farmer’s example: 6 of 60 (10%) vs 8 of 80 (also 10%), so no relationship, yet people attend to the one cell of 6. Chapman & Chapman (1967, 1969): clinicians “saw” paranoia linked to drawing large eyes because they expected it.

Good outcome
Bad outcome
🕯️ Candle
①
②
No candle
③
④
🎣
THINK OF IT LIKE…Fishing in your memory: whatever bites first seems to be what the lake is full of. Recent, famous and personal fish bite fastest.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Many cases where both happened prove a link."
✓ CORRECTCompare cell 1 ÷ (1 + 2) with cell 3 ÷ (3 + 4). One cell is never a correlation.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDAvailability means “if I can think of lots of examples, it must be common”. Usually that works, but recent news, media coverage and your own experiences skew it, which is why both partners think they do most of the chores. It also makes us see links that aren’t there, because we only remember the cases that fit.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKEasy to recall → seems common. One cell isn’t a correlation.
✎ EXAM TIPFor any “why do people overestimate X?” question, ask: is X recent, familiar, vivid, dreaded, or self-performed? Then name the availability heuristic and the specific contaminant.
✅ Quick check: Why can each spouse sincerely claim to do most of the chores?

Your own chores are far more available: you did and experienced them, while many of your partner’s happen when you are not there. Each partner’s own contributions come to mind more easily, so each overestimates their share (Ross & Sicoly, 1979).

✅ Quick check: Why did Oppenheimer and Monin (2009) need the cognitive-load condition?

Normally people deliberately discount fame and pick the non-famous name. Load removes that deliberate thought, revealing the raw availability effect: the famous name was chosen 80% of the time.

✅ Quick check: How can you counteract an availability effect?

Switch from fast, intuitive Type 1 processing to slow, critical Type 2 processing (Kahneman, 2011): “He underestimates the risks of indoor pollution because there are few media stories on them. That’s an availability effect. He should look at the statistics.” Doctors: list alternatives and rule out the worst case (Lambe et al., 2016; Croskerry, 2018).

▶ Find a video: availability heuristic▶ Find a video: illusory correlation
⚓A.5

Anchoring, rescuing base rates, and evaluating the approach

❓ This lecture answers: How do anchors bias estimates, when do people use base rates after all, and what is wrong with the heuristics-and-biases approach?
TRY IT · 5 SECONDS

⚓ Estimate the product

You get one of two versions at random. You have 5 seconds: no calculator!

…
ANCHORS IN REAL LIFE · A.5.1

⚖️ Why does the anchor stick?

Even arbitrary or impossible anchors work (living to 140; a roulette wheel and the number of African countries in the UN: Fiedler & von Sydow, 2015), for experts as well as novices (Mussweiler et al., 2004). Everyday version: “meet at the library in 15 minutes?” You adjust to 20 and still forget your coat, a phone call and a shoelace.

Which anchor makes people adjust their estimate of a TV’s production cost more?

Source: Janiszewski & Uy (2008), in Sternberg.

Likely mechanism
The anchor restricts the memory search to information close to it (Kahneman, 2011; Pohl et al., 2003).
Simpler rival
The anchor just priming similar values: Eysenck & Keane find little evidence for an incomplete-adjustment process.
CALIBRATION TEST · A.5.2

🎯 Give a 90% range for each

Type a low and a high number so you are 90% sure the answer is inside. Well calibrated = about 4–5 hits out of 5. Most people’s ranges are too narrow. illustrative items

The Word example: best guess for the area of Germany 500,000 km² → range 400,000–600,000, too narrow if the anchor is badly off. Matlin’s advice: question your first estimate and ask whether this situation needs a new anchor or a large adjustment.

DIAGRAM · MATLIN & FARMER

🔁 One habit, three errors

A.5.1
Anchoring and adjustment

⚓ Anchoring-and-adjustment heuristic: start from an anchor, but adjustments are too small. 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 → 2,250; 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 × 5 × 6 × 7 × 8 → 512; true answer 40,320 (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).

A.5.2
Confidence intervals that are too narrow

📏 A confidence interval should hold the answer as often as promised, yet 98% intervals hit only ~60% (Block & Harper, 1991): we anchor on a best guess and adjust too little. Students’ “90%” ≈ 50% sure (Teigen & Jørgensen, 2005).

A.5.3
When people do use base rates

🔍 Often they do: .84 vs .53 with 997 vs 3 engineers (Bialek, 2017). Causal knowledge helps (Krynski & Tenenbaum, 2007: faded paint cut neglect from 43% to 8%), and so does motivation (Ditto et al., 1998).

A.5.4
The natural frequency hypothesis

🔢 We meet the world by natural sampling, so counts beat percentages: 16% vs 46% correct (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995); a clear advantage overall (McDowell & Jacobs, 2017); medical students 45% vs 7% (Hoffrage et al., 2015).

A.5.5
Evaluating the heuristics-and-biases approach

⚖️ Hugely influential, and saving effort is real. But (Fiedler & von Sydow, 2015): vague labels, little theoretical progress, biased samples rather than biased processing, emotion ignored, artificial lab tasks.

SIDE BY SIDE · A.5.3

🛟 Three rescues of the base rate

📊 People often use themBialek (2017), 1,000 descriptions: “engineer” judged .84 when 997 were engineers and .53 when only 3 were. Many even used base rates that were irrelevant.
🔧 Causal knowledgeMammogram: in the false-positive version (2% have cancer; 6% of healthy women test positive) base rates were neglected. The benign-cyst version explains the 6%, and base rates were used. Taxi with faded paint (knowing why the witness errs): neglect 43% → 8%, correct 8% → 46%. People use base rates when they see the causal structure.
🎯 MotivationDitto et al. (1998): when blue paper meant illness, people used the 1/10 error rate to call the test inaccurate; when blue meant healthy, the test looked fine. We are motivated to use base rates when it suits us, feeding myside bias.
CRITIQUE · A.5.5

🔍 Five criticisms, five examples

1 · Heuristics are vaguely definedOne-word labels are “theory surrogates” that place no testable constraints on the process.
2 · Theory has made little progressIs anchoring incomplete adjustment or simple priming? When is each heuristic used?
3 · Errors may come from biased samples, not biased processingSkin cancer judged a commoner cause of death than mouth and throat cancer, mainly because of media coverage (Hertwig et al., 2005).
4 · Emotion and motivation were rarely studiedFormaldehyde risk judged higher in a sad mood (Lench & Darbor, 2014).
5 · Laboratory artificialityBase-rate neglect may partly reflect artificial tasks (McDowell & Jacobs, 2017), which leads to the natural-frequency hypothesis.

Strengths to set against them: Kahneman and Tversky founded the field, their ideas spread to economics and philosophy, and people really do minimise effort with heuristics.

🚢
THINK OF IT LIKE…A ship's anchor: you can drift a little, but the chain keeps you close to where you dropped it, even if you dropped it in the wrong place.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Natural frequencies make people perfect Bayesians."
✓ CORRECTThey help a lot (16% → 46% correct) but most people still err. "Clear advantage", not "solves it".
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDAnchoring means you start from a number and don’t move far enough from it, which is why 8×7×6… gets a bigger guess than 1×2×3…, and why our “98% sure” ranges are right only 60% of the time. And people aren’t completely blind to base rates: give them a cause or plain counts and they do much better.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKStart somewhere, stop too soon. Counts beat percentages.
✎ EXAM TIPWhen asked to “evaluate” the heuristics approach, give two strengths (huge influence; effort-saving is real) and two or three of Fiedler and von Sydow’s criticisms (vague labels, weak theory, environmental samples, emotion ignored).
✅ Quick check: How does anchoring produce overly narrow confidence intervals?

We make a best guess (the anchor) and adjust up and down from it too little (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). If the anchor is badly off, the narrow range misses the answer: 98% intervals contain it only about 60% of the time.

✅ Quick check: Rewrite Canvas Question 9 (1% disease, 95% sensitivity, 90% specificity) in natural frequencies.

Of 10,000 people, 100 are ill and 95 test positive; 9,900 are healthy and 990 test positive. So only 95 of 1,085 positives are ill ≈ 9%. In counts the base rate is impossible to ignore: the false positives (990) swamp the true ones (95).

✅ Quick check: What two problems do Eysenck and Keane see in the natural frequency hypothesis?

(1) The frequencies we meet are only a sample and can differ from the population (students meet unusual proportions of highly intelligent people). (2) Word problems with frequency information are not real natural sampling: they bypass its complexities.

Matlin pp. 436–446 · Robinson-Riegler pp. 481–489 (+ Sternberg)

Block C · Decision Making

❓ How should people choose between risky options, how do they actually choose, and are their shortcuts flaws or tools?

🪙C.1

The rational yardstick: expected utility and its violations

❓ This lecture answers: What does a "rational" choice look like, and how do people break its rules?
C.1.1
Expected utility theory

🪙 Expected utility theory: weigh each outcome’s utility (its “good”; Baron, 1999) by its probability. A coin for $40 beats a die for $50. Normative = how we should choose, a baseline; descriptive = how we actually choose.

C.1.2
Invariance and preference reversals

🔄 Invariance: presentation shouldn’t change a choice. Lichtenstein & Slovic (1971, 1973): people play the high-probability gamble but say the high-amount one is worth more, a preference reversal, even in a Las Vegas casino.

C.1.3
Bounded rationality: satisficing and elimination by aspects

⏱️ Bounded rationality (Simon, 1957): we satisfice, more so with limited working memory (Chen & Sun, 2003) and in industry (Chamodrakas et al., 2010). Elimination by aspects (Tversky, 1972), then a careful final choice (Payne, 1976).

INTERACTIVE · PREFERENCE REVERSAL

🎰 Choose, then price

Lichtenstein & Slovic’s example pair. Gamble P: 80% chance to win $4.00, 20% chance to lose $0.50. Gamble $: 10% chance to win $40.00, 90% chance to lose $1.00. Choose one to play, then say what each is worth (your selling price).

Which would you rather play?
Selling price for P ($)
Selling price for $ ($)
INTERACTIVE · ELIMINATION BY ASPECTS

🏫 Pick a college, one aspect at a time

Sternberg’s aspects (cost under $20,000 a year, then West Coast); the colleges are illustrative.

🍬
THINK OF IT LIKE…Buying gum before a train: you grab the first acceptable pack (satisficing). For a medical diagnosis you'd want to weigh everything (expected utility).
✗ THE MISTAKE"Expected utility is wrong because people violate it."
✓ CORRECTExpected utility is a normative model (how a rational agent should choose) and remains a useful yardstick. Violations show it is a poor descriptive model: it assumes too much information, weighing and foresight, which is why prospect theory was developed.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDThe textbook “rational” rule says: weigh how good each outcome is by how likely it is, and don’t let the wording change your mind. People break the second part easily, for example picking one gamble but saying the other is worth more. In real life we also settle for “good enough” instead of the best.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKExpected utility = should. Invariance = same choice, same answer.
✎ EXAM TIPAlways pair a violation with the principle it violates: preference reversals and framing both violate invariance.
▶ Find a video: expected utility▶ Find a video: satisficing
📈C.2

Prospect theory and the framing effect

❓ This lecture answers: How do people value gains and losses, and why does wording flip their choices?
INTERACTIVE · THE VALUE FUNCTION

📈📉 Feel a gain vs a loss

Move the slider. The curve is concave for gains, convex and steeper for losses (schematic, after Robinson-Riegler Fig. 11.4).

TRY IT · ASIAN DISEASE PROBLEM

🦠 600 people at risk

You get one version at random. Choose, then see the classic results.

C.2.1
Value relative to a reference point

📈 Prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979), a descriptive model: value = gain or loss from now. Gains and losses are on different scales: gains grow more slowly; loss aversion. So for gains we avoid risks, for losses we seek risks.

C.2.2
The framing effect: wording

🦠 Asian disease: “200 people will be saved” → 72% choose sure A, 28% the gamble. “400 people will die” → 22% sure C, 78% the gamble D. Only the framing changes: gains → risk averse, losses → risk seeking.

C.2.3
The framing effect: background

🎟️ Background context: lost a €20 ticket → 46% buy another; lost a €20 note → 88% buy one (Matlin’s Demonstration 12.7). Mental accounts, or psychological accounting. Tip: reword big decisions (“how would I feel not having this job?”).

REFRAME IT · C.2.2

🔁 Same fact, two frames

😟 Matlin’s alarming letter
“Opponents have introduced legislation in 17 state governments.”
😌 Same fact, calm frame
Opponents failing to do so in 33 states.

Framing is strong and replicated (Kahneman, 2011), in sophisticated and naive people, young and old (Mayhorn et al., 2002). It shapes medical decisions (McNeil et al., 1986), health behaviours (Rothman & Salovey, 1997), whether to continue a romantic relationship (Boon & Griffin, 1996) and political messages, though it persuades less from low-credibility sources (Druckman, 2001).

A surgeon can say “90% survival” or “10% mortality”. Which wording makes patients more willing?
🥛
THINK OF IT LIKE…Half-full vs half-empty. The glass is the same; "saved" puts you on the gains side (protect what you have), "die" puts you on the losses side (take a chance to avoid it).
✗ THE MISTAKE"People choose differently because the programmes differ."
✓ CORRECTThe programs are identical in outcome and expected value (A = C, B = D). Only the frame (saved vs die) changes the reference point, so the same outcome is coded as a gain or a loss. That is why it violates invariance.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDWe don’t judge outcomes by where we end up, but by whether they feel like a win or a loss compared with now, and losses hurt more. So “200 people will be saved” makes us play safe, but “400 people will die” makes us gamble, even though it’s exactly the same deal.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKGains: play it safe. Losses: roll the dice. Wording sets the reference point.
✎ EXAM TIPLearn the four numbers 72/28 and 22/78, and be able to explain them with the shape of the value function (concave gains, convex and steeper losses).
▶ Find a video: prospect theory▶ Find a video: Asian disease framing
🎟️C.3

Accounts, sunk costs, time, the brain and emotion

❓ This lecture answers: How do mental accounts, past investments, time, effort, stress and touch bend our choices?
VOTE · ARKES & BLUMER (1985)

⛷️ Two non-refundable ski trips, same weekend

Wisconsin cost $50 and will be more enjoyable. Michigan cost $100. Which do you go on?

C.3.1
Psychological accounting

👛 Lost money (a $10 bill)? Most still buy a ticket. Lost the ticket? Less willing: psychological accounting (Kahneman & Tversky, 1981). The lost ticket hits the “play account”. “A little silly”: you are out $20 either way.

C.3.2
Sunk costs

🕳️ Sunk-cost effect: most chose the $100 Michigan trip over the more enjoyable $50 Wisconsin one (Arkes & Blumer, 1985), “throwing good money after bad” (Garland, 1990). Sternberg’s sunk-cost fallacy: repairing a “lemon” car.

C.3.3
Time: the temporal value asymmetry

⏳ Future > past (Caruso et al., 2008): asked before their winter break, people valued it more and would pay more to extend it ($113 vs $91) than people asked after it. Found in all five studies.

C.3.4
Framing in the brain: minimising effort

🧠 fMRI (Gonzalez et al., 2005): mainly frontal and parietal activity. The brain was less active for the certain option in the gain frame and for the risky one in the loss frame: we minimise cognitive effort.

C.3.5
Emotion: stress and touch

🧊 A hand in ice-cold water (stress) accentuated framing (more System 1): risky choices .42 → .33 for gains, .61 → .66 for losses (Porcelli & Delgado, 2009). A woman’s touch on the shoulder raised risky investing to $3.44 (Levav & Argo, 2010).

DIAGRAM · GONZALEZ ET AL. (2005)

🧠 The preferred option is the easy one

👛
THINK OF IT LIKE…Labelled envelopes for money. Losing the "concert envelope" money feels like the concert just got pricier; losing cash from your wallet doesn't, even though you're €20 down either way.
✗ THE MISTAKEMixing up which ticket problem is "Problem 1".
✓ CORRECTMatlin’s Problem 1 = lost ticket; Robinson-Riegler’s scenario 1 = lost money. In both books people are less willing to buy after losing the ticket (Matlin: 46% vs 88%). Name the scenario, not the number.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDWe keep money in mental pockets: losing a ticket feels like the concert got pricier, losing cash doesn’t. We stick with things because we’ve already paid for them, value future fun more than past fun, pick whichever option is easier for the brain, and gamble more under stress or after a friendly touch on the shoulder.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKPockets, sunk costs, future > past, easy > effortful, stress and touch tilt risk.
✎ EXAM TIPFor sunk-cost questions, always say what a rational chooser would do: ignore money already spent, because it is gone whatever you choose.

😎C.4

Overconfidence, hindsight, and biases or adaptive tools?

❓ This lecture answers: How do we misjudge our own judgements, and are heuristics flaws or tools?
MATLIN’S FIVE REASONS · C.4.1

🤔 Why are we overconfident?

1 · Shaky foundationsWe don’t realise our knowledge rests on shaky assumptions and unreliable sources.
2 · Easy confirmationsConfirming examples are readily available; we don’t search for counterexamples.
3 · No rivals in mindWe can’t recall competing hypotheses.
4 · Rivals not taken seriouslyEven when we recall alternatives, we dismiss them.
5 · Never taughtWe don’t pause to switch from Type 1 to Type 2 thinking.

It is everywhere: researchers and their theories (Trout, 2002); phone contracts that profit from overestimated usage (Grubb, 2009); 77% of students overconfident, 23% not (Stanovich, 1999); Chinese participants most confident, Japanese least (Yates, 2010). Political decisions: each side in a conflict expects to win (Johnson, 2004); Iraq WMD evidence turned out to be a forgery (Tavris & Aronson, 2007). Crystal-ball technique: imagine a perfect crystal ball shows your favoured explanation is wrong, then generate alternatives (Cannon-Bowers & Salas, 1998).

INTERACTIVE · PLANNING FALLACY

📅 How long will your next essay take?

Estimate in hours. Then apply two of Matlin’s remedies (split the task; think of someone else’s obstacles) and see your new estimate. illustrative

Causes: we imagine an optimistic scenario, recall finishing similar tasks quickly, and expect more free time in the future (Zauberman & Lynch, 2005). Remedies: divide the project (Forsyth & Burt, 2008), envision and rehearse each step (Taylor et al., 1998), imagine how long someone else took, obstacles included (Buehler et al., 2012).

First guess (hours)
C.4.1
Overconfidence

😎 Overconfidence: 100% sure, 80% right (Fischhoff et al., 1977). It shows in political decisions (Iraq) and the planning fallacy (Buehler et al., 2002). Remedy: the crystal-ball technique. Dangerous form: my-side bias (Stanovich, 2009).

C.4.2
The hindsight bias

🔙 Hindsight bias: “knew it all along” (Hastie & Dawes, 2010); we rebuild the past (Schacter, 2001). Carli (1999): each ending felt predictable. Explanation: anchoring and adjustment on the known outcome (Pohl et al., 2002). It hinders learning (Biais & Weber, 2009).

C.4.3
Biases or adaptive tools?

🧰 Kahneman–Tversky (KT): why do we fall short? Gigerenzer: an adaptive toolbox for bounded rationality, fast and frugal, ecological rationality: recognition, take-the-best, default (28% vs 99.9% donors). Both agree heuristics usually serve us well.

DIAGRAM · C.4.3

🔭 One set of heuristics, two lenses

INTERACTIVE · THE DEFAULT HEURISTIC

🫀 Same people, different default

illustrative simulation Imagine 400 citizens who all "do nothing" unless they care strongly (say 1 in 20 acts). Switch the system and see who ends up as a donor.

QUIZ · RECOGNITION HEURISTIC

🏙️ Which city is larger?

Milan vs Modena is the readings’ example; the other pairs are illustrative.

🔭
THINK OF IT LIKE…Kahneman & Tversky inspect the toolbox for broken tools; Gigerenzer watches the tools working on real jobs. Same tools, different question.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Hindsight bias and overconfidence are the same thing."
✓ CORRECTOverconfidence is about current judgements and predictions (too sure now). Hindsight bias is about the past (after the outcome, believing you would have predicted it). Matlin links them: hindsight is overconfidence about our past predictive ability.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDBefore deciding, we’re too sure of ourselves, like estimating 10 hours for a paper that takes 30. After the outcome, we think we knew it all along. But mental shortcuts aren’t simply bugs: in the real world, simple rules like “go with the one you recognise” or “stick with the default” often work really well.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKToo sure before, “knew it” after; shortcuts are tools, not just traps.
✎ EXAM TIPIn any “biases or adaptive?” question, end with the consensus: both views agree heuristics generally serve us well, and the disagreement is about emphasis and the yardstick (normative rules vs fit with the environment).
✅ Quick check: How can anchoring and adjustment explain the hindsight bias?

Knowing the outcome happened (100% certain) is the anchor. When people estimate what they would have predicted beforehand, they adjust down from it too little. Memory reconstruction, as in Carli’s (1999) false memories, adds to it.

🧵 Synthesis: the rule, the shortcut, the rescue

Block A–B (judgement)Block C (decision making)
📐 Normative standardBayes; conjunction ruleExpected utility; invariance
🧰 What we doRepresentativeness, availability, anchoringProspect theory: gains vs losses, loss aversion
⚠️ Signature errorBase-rate neglect; conjunction fallacyFraming effects; preference reversals; sunk costs
🖼️ Presentation mattersFrequencies and causal stories helpWording and background change choices
🪞 Judging ourselvesToo-narrow confidence intervalsOverconfidence; planning fallacy; hindsight bias
🌱 The positive viewRecognition heuristic; natural frequenciesTake-the-best; default heuristic; ecological rationality
The same mind that neglects base rates and flips with wording does much better with counts, causal stories, reworded questions, alternatives to consider and time to switch from Type 1 to Type 2 thinking.

📄 Theme 6 on one page

🚕A1

Judging & the ideal

Judgement = how likely; decision = what to choose. Bayes: combine how common something is with how strong the clue is (taxi-cab: 41%, not 80%).
👔A2

Representativeness

We ignore base rates and judge by resemblance: Jack “is” an engineer, random-looking births seem likelier, one anecdote beats statistics, gamblers feel “due”.
🏦A3

Conjunction fallacy

Extra detail feels likelier but can’t be (Linda); even 49% of doctors (double fallacy). Frequencies reduce it.
💭A4

Availability

Easy to recall → seems common; skewed by recency, familiarity, media, dread; recognition can help; one-cell thinking → illusory correlation.
⚓A5

Anchoring; rescue; critique

Start somewhere, adjust too little (2,250 vs 512; narrow intervals). Base rates used with causes, motives, frequencies. The approach is vague and lab-bound.
🪙C1

Expected utility

Rational ideal: value × probability, and invariance. Preference reversals break it; real people satisfice.
📈C2

Prospect theory & framing

Gains vs losses from a reference point; losses hurt more; safe for gains, risky for losses (72% vs 78%); background framing (46% vs 88%).
🎟️C3

Accounts & feelings

Mental pockets, sunk costs, future > past, the least-effort option; stress and touch increase risk tendencies.
😎C4

Confidence & the debate

Too sure before (planning fallacy), “knew it” after (Carli). Gigerenzer: heuristics are fast, frugal tools that fit real environments; both camps agree they mostly work.
💬 The whole theme to a friend: “When we guess how likely things are, we use shortcuts: does it look typical, can I think of examples, where did I start? They usually work, but they make us forget how common things are, believe detailed stories, and stay too close to first guesses. When we choose, we don’t weigh outcomes coolly: we ask whether they feel like wins or losses, so ‘200 saved’ and ‘400 die’ get different answers. We’re also too sure of ourselves, and afterwards we think we knew it all along. But give people plain counts, a causal story or a familiar setting, and their shortcuts look pretty smart.”

Sources: Eysenck & Keane Ch. 13 · Matlin & Farmer Ch. 12 · Sternberg, Sternberg & Mio Ch. 12 · Matlin Ch. 12 · Robinson-Riegler & Robinson-Riegler Ch. 11. Video buttons open a YouTube search so you can pick a current video.
